mr president, nowadays we are faced with a paradox. although a majority of european consumers have repeatedly stated that they are against gmos, surveys show that they do buy gm foods when they are available in supermarkets. many consumers are just not aware that gm food is sold in europe or simply fall into the trap of illegible labels and end up not knowing what they buy. a possible solution would be to allow the absence of gmo in foods to be mentioned on the label. but currently there are no common provisions on gm-free labelling, leaving the member states the freedom of choice. this leads to confusion of consumers and distortion of the internal market since, while some countries have already introduced non-gm labelling provisions, others refuse to allow this kind of information to be given. people want to make food choices based on their own values and not according to safety assessment studies. if we care about consumers’ concerns, then we should be transparent all the way and give them a real choice. therefore i call on the commission to provide the legal framework for voluntary gm-free labelling at european level.
mr president, the gas crisis has left hundreds of thousands of households across 17 european countries without heating during freezing temperatures. eastern and central europe have been affected the most by the dispute, which has shut down factories and schools. even if kiev and moscow sign the eu-brokered deal after hours of talks with eu officials, gazprom says that the deal to restart gas supplies to europe via ukraine will be delayed as it has not received a copy of the agreement. the team of technical experts sent by the european commission will check flows into ukrainian pipelines from russia and, even if the gas starts to flow in ukraine, it may take about 36 hours to reach eu member states. as a result, europe needs a single policy on energy security in order to avoid future conflicts and it needs to diversity its sources of energy supplies. i welcome the intervention of parliament in the dispute and hope that an agreement will be reached as soon as possible in order to avoid a deepening conflict.
there was a lot of talk, including tonight, about the gas crisis. it is always said how serious and dangerous the level of energy dependence of the european union is. it is repeated every time that the solution is to further reduce dependence on single sources of energy. but we must not forget another imperative, that of energy conservation. what the level of energy waste in the european union is at this moment is hard to say. some analysts are talking about as much as a third of the total consumption. as an example, i can say that if romania's imports of russian gas are about 14 million tons of oil equivalent per year, almost 1 million tons of oil equivalent per year are wasted because of the poor insulation of housing blocks. unfortunately, community legislation is not designed to help solve this problem, because it inexplicably limits the european funds that can be allocated to thermal rehabilitation projects. i think we should ask ourselves every day the question: what is simpler? should we look for new sources of energy, should we look for new transit routes, or should we not forget that by simple methods we can save a good deal of wasted energy?
the european union must give priority to the development of a common energy strategy and an action plan to improve the union's energy security. the interruption of natural gas supplies to the member states of the union via ukraine has shown the union's dependence on its traditional suppliers. the cold temperatures this winter have also caused serious operational problems for electricity suppliers, which have recorded historic consumption figures. the union must develop a european strategy for modernising the energy grid, increasing energy efficiency and diversifying energy supply sources. the nabucco project, the construction of liquefied gas terminals in european ports, investment in safer nuclear power plants, increased energy efficiency and the increased use of renewable energy should be among the common priority actions dedicated to increasing the union's energy security. the european commission, together with the european investment bank and the governments of the member states, must identify and ensure the financing of these priority projects.
and since this year, 2009, is just beginning, i would like to tell you all that, in my opinion, it is not an ordinary year. in 2009, two decades have passed since the end of the cold war and the breaking down of all the walls that divided countries and europe, east and west, into freedom and democracy on the one hand and totalitarian regimes on the other. as a romanian mp, but also as a romanian citizen who has known the dictatorship, i believe that these two decades have meant for some of us a transition, and for the other part, acceptance. i also believe that, despite the context, 2009 should be the year in which our action, and the european commission's action as well, consecrates a europe for all europeans: a europe in which each of the 500 million europeans feels that his rights are guaranteed, that solidarity is real, that no one can be discriminated against, that no one should feel alienated or tolerated in a united europe, that we are all european citizens who feel the same, no matter where we were before 1989.
the use of plant protection products in accordance with efficient agricultural practices is essential for the production of sufficient quantities of quality food, which offers a high level of protection of consumer health and the environment. reducing the risk and impact associated with the use of pesticides and setting targets to reduce the frequency of their use will help to ensure sustainable agriculture. the presence of high levels of pesticides in food consumed in the european union is the result of a dependence on these chemicals, which, although necessary for pest control and increased production yields, can have negative effects on public health. some member states, including romania, are facing a high degree of infestation of agricultural land, with the use of pesticides being the apparent best method of pest control. for this reason, the proposals for the implementation of integrated pesticide management, the use of alternative substances and risk management will encourage the production of appropriate agricultural products, which take into account the environment and the safety of public health, thus reducing dependence on plant protection products. at the same time, the large number of pests on romanian agricultural land forces us to use in-flight treatments. however, once the directive enters into force, such spraying will only take place when no viable alternative pest control solutions are available to ensure a sufficient level of environmental protection. i am pleased with the outcome of the compromise, which has the support of most political groups and which ensures a balance between the availability of plant protection products and, by implication, a sufficient quantity of food, maintaining the competitiveness of european farmers and increasing environmental and health protection.
in writing. – i support the compromise of the breyer report on the placing of plant protection products on the market because it will provide for greater stability and security for farmers and food producers. however, the compromise agreement states that the new legislation would only gradually replace the existing eu law, and that pesticides already approved under current rules would remain available until their existing authorisation expires. products that contain hazardous substances are to be replaced within three years if safer alternatives exist. if voted, the report will be a step towards better health through environmental protection and a means of allowing the eu to move on to a better system without further delays.
in writing. i welcome the text of the compromise on the sustainable use of pesticides and i would like to congratulate mrs klaß on her work. i believe that we have a balanced text here, which prohibits the use of harmful pesticides without harming european agriculture. i am also pleased to note that the non-chemical methods of plant protection and pest and crop management do not include the use of gmos as an alternative. there would have been a possibility to include them among the non-chemical methods. this would have opened a door for the future marketing of food containing gmos on the union market. the text of the compromise proves that this is not the case. once again, the european parliament says a decisive no to the use of gmos. the united voice of 58% of european citizens is thus being heard once again. this time we have the member states, represented by the council, with us.
in writing. pesticide regulations are important to reduce the risks to human health and the environment from their use. however, measures taken to this end must be reasonable and take into account both the quality of production and the maximisation of harvests. in the context of the economic crisis, increasing food production may be a solution. as mrs mcguinness noted in her report to the agriculture committee at the end of last year, the price of wheat has risen by 180% in two years, and food prices in general have risen globally by 83%. these high prices are generated by the high standards we impose on european producers. without contesting the need for better regulation of pesticide use, i nevertheless believe that some of the proposed measures will lead to a reduction in the number of plant protection products on the eu market. as a result, productivity in some sectors will decline, such as cereals. certain provisions of this legislation will affect producers by resulting in the prohibition of most pesticides on the market, favouring instead the marketing of products considered safer but also much more expensive. this will increase production costs, with farmers in the new member states being the most disadvantaged.

eu and provides a comprehensive overview of the issues at stake in eu-western balkans economic and trade relations. allow me to focus on some points highlighted in your report. the western balkans, as perspective of eu membership can act as a catalyst for sustainable economic development and for securing peace and stability within the region. the commission also agrees that the individual fulfilment of the copenhagen criteria is of the utmost importance when judging the readiness of countries in the region to join the eu. the eu is the western balkans’ main trading partner. deeper economic ties between the eu and the region are therefore vital for boosting the region’s economic growth. as rightly pointed out in your report, trade liberalisation and integration is a cornerstone in the stabilisation and association process, and the eu has pursued this objective with the western balkans at three levels. firstly, at the bilateral level, the eu has granted unilateral trade preferences to the western balkans since 2000 so as to facilitate the access of their exports to the eu markets. the commission has negotiated free trade agreements as part of the stabilisation and association agreements to create the conditions for political and economic reforms and to set the basis for the integration of the western balkans into the eu, for example by means of alignment to the acquis. secondly, at the regional level, the european commission acted as a facilitator in the negotiations on the central european free trade agreement (cefta) and decided to provide financial support and technical assistance to the cefta secretariat and to the parties to help implement the agreement. at the same time, the european commission values highly the regional ownership of the agreement and acknowledges that cefta is fundamental for deeper regional economic integration and for preparing the ground for the eventual full participation of the western balkans in the eu single market. moreover, cefta created all the necessary structures to discuss trade-related issues at the regional and bilateral level. this is essential for facilitating and deepening regional cooperation and good neighbourly relations. the european commission will continue to monitor implementation of the cefta and will continue to report on this in its yearly report on the accession and pre-accession process. thirdly, at the multilateral level the commission has supported the accession of the countries in the region to the world trade organisation as this is an absolutely fundamental step for effective participation in the globalised economy. the eu has mobilised all available policy instruments to support the countries of the western balkans in their endeavours for reforms and regional cooperation. the instrument for pre-accession assistance is important for addressing the region’s long term development needs. the total funding for the current financial framework for 2007-2013 is eur 11.5 billion. last but not least, the european commission has started dialogues with all the countries concerned in the region to establish roadmaps for lifting the visa regime. in the light of what has been said, let me assure you that the commission is taking all the necessary steps to enhance trade relations and to bring the western balkans’ economy as close as possible to the eu. in conclusion, i wish to congratulate the rapporteur again for this good report and i am pleased to say that the commission shares its general approach.

in writing. the global food crisis, driven by the continuing rise in the price of maize, wheat and energy, global population growth and climate change, has generated a series of tensions and uprisings that, if not resolved in the near future, could contribute to the destabilisation of countries and regions worldwide. the gap between the rate of population growth that could reach over 9 billion people in 2050 and the shrinking global food supply is alarming. such a situation will most likely lead to the replacement of conflicts over oil with those over clean water and food, respectively, and the struggle for survival. the european union is currently the world's largest donor of humanitarian aid, but food supplies are running out and developing countries, particularly in africa, need more support to tackle chronic poverty and hunger. reducing agriculture's dependence on fossil fuels, using organic products, preserving fertile soils and adapting the common agricultural policy to the food crisis are some of the most important elements to be considered in order to overcome this impasse.

member of the commission. − mr president, the commission welcomes the report presented and the support given to our perspectives regarding the ecosystem approach. one of the main messages the commission gives in its communication is that, while fisheries depend on healthy marine ecosystems, fisheries management cannot take on the role of overall ocean management on its own. healthy marine ecosystems can only be safeguarded through a policy which involves all sectors which impact on these ecosystems. this is why the commission sees the maritime policy, and especially its environmental pillar, the marine strategy directive, as key to the implementation of an ecosystem approach. this approach will give assurances to the fishing industry that all human impacts on marine ecosystems, not only fisheries, are addressed in a proportionate and coherent way. this is also the overall thrust of the report and we appreciate the agreement on this point. i will emphasise that this does not mean that one policy is subordinate to another – that we, by taking this approach are establishing a hierarchy between, for instance, the marine strategy directive and the common fisheries policy. the marine strategy directive serves the common fisheries policy by being the necessary integrative instrument to safeguard the resource base for fisheries in the future, and the common fisheries policy will contribute to the marine strategy directive by putting in place management measures necessary to support the objectives for healthy marine ecosystems. as stated in the report, meeting food needs, safeguarding fishing industries and fishing communities, and preserving the sustainability of marine ecosystems are not irreconcilable. on the contrary, in the long term there is a synergy between these objectives. the report touches on many questions regarding the specific instruments to be utilised in the future. these are important and pertinent questions which we will address in the debate regarding the reform of the common fisheries policy. i will therefore not comment specifically on these questions here. i will, however, point out that there are a couple of points where we may be in disagreement. it is indicated that fishermen affected by management plans and measures to protect ecosystems should be subsidised or compensated. we do not think that direct subsidies is a way forward, but that the solution is to help the industry to be more economically resilient and to help coastal communities diversify into other economic activities. it is also indicated that restocking from aquaculture may be an instrument to replenish wild fish stocks. although this may be an option in a few very specific cases, we do not think that this is the way forward in general. fish stocks should be rebuilt by proper management of the human impacts on the marine ecosystems, including the impacts of both fisheries and other sectors. we will return to a more detailed debate on the instruments for fisheries management in the context of the debate and development of the common fisheries policy reform, starting with our publication of a green paper in april. in the mean time, i thank parliament for its support for our approach as expressed through this report.
in writing. fish stocks in eu waters are declining both because of overfishing and poorly managed gear, and because of the impact of other sectors on marine biological life, especially tourism. scientific research to identify the factors influencing marine ecosystems, including the impact of climate change, will ensure that it is possible to determine the evolution of fisheries resources and take precautionary measures to prevent the rapid and continuous depletion of fish stocks. as fishing is an essential activity for ensuring food and human survival, the management of sustainable fisheries resources becomes fundamental in the context of the deterioration of marine biodiversity. for this reason, the social, economic and environmental components must be taken into account in all initiatives for the sustainable development of coastal areas in the european union.

i congratulate mr carlos coelho on this report. i welcome this initiative, which represents real progress following the thessaloniki european council, by linking the travel document to its holder and by adopting the 'one person, one passport' principle. i would like to stress three important points. first, the need to apply the principles and exceptions set out in this report to the results and problems encountered in practice. the emphasis should therefore be on the three-year review period set by the commission as the timeframe within which both the member states and the commission must try to identify recommendations between theoretical principles and practical impediments. secondly, there is a serious problem with regard to the security of the data stored and the protection of the identity of the holder. finally, i would like to draw attention to the need to develop common principles for the documents required for the issuing of travel documents or passports, this stage being essential both for ensuring the security of databases and for preventing the falsification of these documents.
romania introduced the use of biometric passports as of 1 january 2009. this type of passport has 50 security features and includes for the first time in the european union both facial and fingerprint identification. romania has thus taken an important step towards joining the schengen area, scheduled for 2011. the introduction of biometric passports cancels the last substantive condition for romania's inclusion in the visa waiver program. consequently, the refusal of visa exemption for romanians to the united states is henceforth based on purely subjective grounds and i hope that the united states will take this into account. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur once again on the important improvements he has made to the regulation, in particular the creation of a uniform european system for checking the compatibility of biometric elements with data stored on a chip.
the harmonisation of security standards for biometric passports at european level is an extension of the provisions of the schengen acquis. the regulation provides for a general obligation to provide fingerprints, which are stored on a contactless chip in the passport. i support the exceptions to the provision of fingerprints for children under 12 and call for the revision and harmonisation of specific national legislation. i consider that the processing of data contained in biometric passports must be carried out in compliance with community legislation on the protection of personal data and privacy. the commission and the member states should take the necessary measures to ensure this with regard to the processing of biometric passport data, both at the border and in the process of maintaining the related databases, where national law so provides. however, i would point out that limiting the validity of a biometric passport for persons whose fingerprints are temporarily or permanently unavailable to 12 months or less makes life more difficult for people with disabilities and i ask the commission to re-evaluate the relevant text.
in writing. the threat of terrorism has led to the need to introduce additional security and biometric features to ensure greater protection for passengers travelling within the european union. the most important elements of the proposed regulation are the fight against child trafficking by introducing the 'one person, one passport' principle and the introduction of exemptions for fingerprinting children under 12. however, the legislation of some member states provides for the provision of fingerprints from children under 12 years of age, but this will only be possible for a transitional period of 4 years, the age limit being, however, not to exceed 6 years. certain pilot studies carried out by member states have shown that the fingerprints of children under the age of 6 years are not of good quality and may change during growth. by setting an age limit, the risk of fingerprinting being used to misidentify a person is reduced and the possibility of child trafficking is made more difficult. the need to protect travellers has become increasingly evident since the events of 11 september 2001, but the increased level of security protection must be accompanied by the safeguarding of the rights and dignity of passengers, as laid down in the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
the european union is founded on the principle of transparency, to which the treaty on european union refers in articles 1 and 6 and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union in article 41. from the outset, europe has promoted decision-making that is as transparent and as close to the citizen as possible. the european parliament, by its nature, is the first to promote public access to the decision-making process, with differing opinions on legislative and non-legislative work contributing to the confidence of european citizens in the european institutions. at the moment, public access to documents of the european institutions is quite good. it is clear, however, that the 2001 european legislation governing this right of access needs to be updated. the parliament has asked the commission since 2006 to submit proposals to amend the regulation, making several recommendations: - all documents used to draft legal acts to be directly accessible to the public and - the establishment of a single access point to documents used to draft legislation. the commission took account of these recommendations, which were, moreover, included in the new 2008 proposal for a regulation. during the decision-making process, the parties are confronted with diverse, sometimes contradictory opinions. negotiations lead to the best decision acceptable to all. the european citizen must be informed about the whole process leading to the adoption of decisions, because these decisions directly affect his life.
i would like to point out that, while mr cappato initially had an initiative with broad support, the 18 amendments introduced subsequently led to a loss of initial support. i would argue, however, that public access to parliament, council and commission documents is essential to bringing the european union closer to its citizens. i would first of all like to stress the need to publish the main documents in the comitology procedure. secondly, i think that the amendments tabled by the member in the parliamentary committees to which he belongs should also be published on the website of the european parliament, in the personal file of each member's activities. the citizen must be able to see clearly what amendments the mep has tabled in the european decision-making process, alongside reports, resolutions, plenary speeches. thirdly, the european council, when acting as a co-legislating institution alongside parliament, should publish its debates as parliament publishes its own. the council should be transparent by publishing its debates now, before the lisbon treaty requires it to do so.

the commission's vice-president - madam president, i therefore reply to mr ó neachtain's question. the commission has been pursuing a policy to combat cybercrime for several years. it does so in close cooperation with the member states and the other institutions of the european union. the commission contributes to the fight against cybercrime in four ways: by promoting cooperation between member states, by facilitating public-private partnerships, by developing different legal instruments and, finally, by engaging in cooperation with third countries. the 2007 communication 'towards a comprehensive policy on combating cybercrime' enabled the commission to promote the exchange of information in the field of cybercrime between member states' law enforcement agencies, either bilaterally or via europol. member states should designate permanent contact points through which other member states may request assistance or information. the commission also contributed to the council conclusions on a strategy to combat cybercrime, adopted last november. the strategy proposes a series of measures to encourage cooperation between member states to combat crimes such as child pornography, terrorism, attacks on information systems and fraud. a platform for reporting offences detected on the internet should be set up to centralise cybercrimes in order to allow them to be aggregated by europol. at the same time, the commission is developing a policy of partnership between law enforcement and the private sector to tackle cybercrime. the jai council of 8 december 2008 made recommendations on public-private cooperation against cybercrime. the commission also wants to set up a european financial coalition against commercial child pornography. the aim of this coalition is to combine the efforts of different public and private actors to combat the production, distribution and sale of child pornography images on the internet. finally, the commission has been heavily involved in the development of legislation which sets minimum standards for the harmonization of appropriate criminal legislation. this is the case with framework decision 2005/222/jha on attacks against information systems and framework decision 2004/68/jha on combating the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography. the commission is now studying how to update and put these instruments into practice. i conclude by saying that it is important to remember that the internet is a global information network. the european union cannot come up with regulations on its own. that is why the commission wants to promote international cooperation in this area and we will be organising a meeting with international organisations and european union agencies this year to try to coordinate the respective activities of these international organisations and european union agencies. this is what i can say to mr ó neachtain.

mr president, the problem we are coping with is not a mere russia-ukraine dispute. there is a europe-russia dispute having as its object the geopolitical status of ukraine, a european union-ukraine dispute having as its object the european perspectives of ukraine, a european union-russia dispute having as its object the russian monopoly on the gas supply and a european union-ukraine dispute having as its object the ukrainian monopoly on gas transit. all these disputes combined place us in the middle of an energy war, which is about power-sharing. in this war we are not hostages but combatants. we are not mediators but one of the sides having a legitimate interest. this war extends its consequences from one crisis to another. could we cease the combat and organise a peace conference? we need rules for a free energy market shared by our russian and ukrainian partners. we need guarantees and mechanisms to enhance these rules and an arbitration system for dispute settlement as well as an institution to put in motion those mechanisms. we need a common european energy policy, served by appropriate legal and political instruments and consolidated by an integrated agreement with the supply and transit countries, russia and ukraine respectively. sanctions cannot work. confrontation is not the solution either. let us be united and negotiate strategically and comprehensively. to this end, we have to organise an interparliamentary ad hoc working group formed by european parliament, russian duma and ukrainian rada representatives to follow the process of consensus and strategy-building on a permanent basis as long as necessary.

better equipped, even in that particular region, for that kind of emergency situation. however, i think we should also be aware of the fact that, for example, you cannot build gas storage facilities wherever you want. you need the right kind of a geological environment. for example, we are fortunate in my country that all storage facilities are located in the eastern part of the country. we can pump from those storages and distribute gas even if there is almost no supply from outside. we are able to survive for a few weeks or months, but no longer. on the other hand, slovakia unfortunately has those geological positions in the western part of the country and to reverse the flow is not an easy operation. you need to have the compressors on the pipelines and, if you do not, then it causes trouble. to those who argue that this is a political problem: concerning speaking with one voice, i can tell you from all my experience that of course it is a political problem. it is a political problem because people are freezing so it is a politically difficult situation. of course i agree with those, like jacek saryusz-wolski or istván szent-iványi, who argue that this is a kind of cynical game and, in fact, at the heart of this is the fight about who is going to control the infrastructure in the country in question. others, like hannes swoboda and jan marinus wiersma, stress that we should not take a black-and-white approach to this and that ukraine deserves some attention – you are also right: of course ukraine is not making this easier. that is, at least, my own view. but then we should be aware of the fact that bulgaria and slovakia are in a terrible situation, because suddenly there is a country that wants to exploit this difficult situation and to put those countries into conflict with ukraine. that is what we can see right now, from the developments today, for example. so it is difficult – what can we do? then there are those who are afraid to enter into the game at all because they view it as being like the card game schwarzer peter, with the danger that whoever ends up with the black card will foot the bill. i do not think that the one who is afraid to play is courageous. i think a courageous person is one is willing to take a risk. why not buy gas on the ukrainian-russian border? an excellent example! we have discussed this, but who are the contractors on the eu side? they are private companies who are afraid because they do not have control over the gas coming in. there obviously should be a solution but that would require the willingness of ukraine to give up a stake in the pipeline. as you know, their parliament prohibits that and they are not ready to do it. european companies should take a certain role, and there is nothing that can be done in a matter of weeks or even months. so we need to step up the pressure. but today, for example, we said that legal action must follow here. i think this is important on both sides. i do not want to repeat myself and again take longer than i should. i want to thank you above all for your interest and your active attitude – from jacek saryusz-wolski, the ppe-de group, to all of you here. we need your help and your attention. we need your help in drawing attention to this issue to those in european countries where this is not a problem on the front pages. that is mostly in this part of member of the commission. − madam president, honourable members, i will just say a couple of things. first of all, our task is to restore supplies immediately because people are suffering, industry is suffering, people are losing jobs; so that is the main task, not to create additional obstacles. but, after that, an analysis should take place, and measures should also be taken. we should revisit some of our stereotypes, because if 2006 could be called a wake-up call, this is a real shock. in reality we are underestimating what really happened. if two countries’ governments have accused each other of turning off the tap of the gas pipelines, then the only conclusion that i can draw – because i trust the countries and governments – is that somebody tampered with the pipelines, and that is very difficult to believe. so what has happened is really extraordinary and i believe it should have a huge impact on the energy policies that we are trying to create. that is why i believe that no issue should be taboo any more. we really should discuss how to guarantee security of supply under all possible conditions. and, to be honest, i never expected full disruption of supply. it was never in my expectations: it was a shock for me too. you can blame me as energy commissioner, and say ‘you should have foreseen this’. but it was never to be expected. it is something new that never has happened before and we should in future be prepared for such a type of measure.
in writing. the european union is again facing a natural gas supply crisis. it's not clear who the culprit is. russia, the ukraine? both of you? i ask the european commission to inform the public about the reasons that have led to this situation. the european union must take responsibility for saying who is really to blame. the crisis has shown that, unfortunately, many of the eu countries are vulnerable to energy blackmail and may suffer from political rather than economic disagreements between the countries of the former soviet union. it is clear that we need to accelerate the process of creating a common european energy policy, based also on a common external approach. we need to accelerate the process of diversifying natural gas supply sources and transport routes, and accelerating the nabucco project is essential. i think that a report by the energy commissioner is required on the actions taken or, more correctly, 'not taken' by the commission to support the nabucco project over the last year.
in writing. the gas crisis highlights two major problems facing the european union. we have no common energy strategy because there is no cohesion. now, the supply cuts have affected 11 of the 27 eu countries. but dependence on russian gas is a common security concern, given that the energy weapon can be used at any time, especially against former russian satellites. in these circumstances, the eu has a duty to find a solution to secure the energy supply of the new member states. the real problem for europe is diversifying gas sources, not transit routes between russia and the eu. secondly, the gas crisis shows the political weakness of a divided and hesitant european union. one of the obvious shortcomings is the eu presidency. there is a need, especially in times of crisis, for a representative voice to speak for the union. a chorus of voices risks casting aspersions on the idea of a united europe, not just its international image and influence. this is why we need a european presidency for a longer period and independence from the political structures of the member states.
in writing. – another wake-up call. the current gas crisis shows once more how weak and ineffective our eu energy policy is. when under big pressure eu national governments rely, basically, on their own resources and sources. this is not surprising under the circumstances, but it shows another facet of lack of eu solidarity. this crisis also highlights what is a must for future steps in eu energy policy if we wish to have one, in reality. as for oil stocks we should develop gas storage. we need to diversify gas suppliers, supply routes and delivery mechanisms (as in the case of liquefied natural gas). the construction of the nabucco project should be speeded up and the money for this project should be enhanced by involving the eib in its funding. the argument that not enough gas would be available were new transport routes to be developed does not stand scrutiny. we need to develop renewable energy resources at a faster pace and save energy. last, but not least, we need to develop cross-border energy interconnectors, so that eu member states can help each other if need arises.
in writing. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen,the energy sector is a major economic and geopolitical factor; today almost half of the eu's energy is imported, and forecasts show that imports could reach 70% for natural gas and 100% for oil by 2030. these must be the main reasons for the urgent need to establish a common energy policy. they must base the implementation of the common energy policy on three pillars: the interconnection of national networks throughout the union, the diversification of sources of supply and active energy saving measures. the eu's energy policy is based on the principle of the 'one country, two systems' principle, which is the basis for the eu's energy policy. can gas be stolen from a network like a wallet from a pocket? can the gas be stopped in a few minutes without notifying the user? i think that before we look at the non-compliance with international treaties and agreements and the fact that the supplier, which receives most of its revenues from gas exports, treats europeans who pay conscientiously for this gas with "coldness" and disinterestedness, we must look at the solutions for the eu's energy security.

in writing. the issue of russian gas supplies to ukraine and the european union must be resolved as soon as possible. the european union needs a policy of energy security, diversification of resources and solidarity in the energy sector to prevent such crises affecting its citizens. more than half of the eu member states are affected by the russian gas supply cut. in bulgaria, gas supplies to industry have been reduced or cut off, as the country is 90% dependent on gas from russia. i support both the presidency and the commission's position to encourage both sides to dialogue in order to reach a compromise. without technical coordination between the two parties, the gas supply cannot be carried out. in the future, we must keep the dialogue open with both sides to avoid such situations. the council and parliament, through the energy package under discussion, are proposing a series of measures involving the existence of several energy suppliers for the benefit of the consumer, a package which we hope will be adopted at second reading. this crisis must be resolved as soon as possible as it affects both european citizens and european industry; we need a common external energy policy.

the european union has multiple responsibilities in somalia and the horn of africa. instability, lack of governance, and insecurity have made this region a source of concern for a number of reasons. first of all, the unprecedented growth in acts of piracy by groups sheltered in somali ports is affecting trade routes in a region that is vital to european and global economic exchanges. we note with concern that these groups are becoming more technologically sophisticated and capable of attacking ships at greater and greater distances from shore. obviously, this is due to the desperate situation in somalia, in this case the lack of a central government capable of controlling its territorial waters. but equally, the international community has a responsibility in relation to these events. piracy, no matter what seas it takes place in and what safe havens it enjoys, violates the written and unwritten laws of every country and an intervention against it is justified no matter which direction it comes from. the chances of the european union and the international community fundamentally changing the reality in somalia are slim. but let's fight one of its effects - piracy. it's much more accessible.

in writing. kenyan democracy suffered a blow to press freedom in early 2009. president mwai kibaki signed, after a change of heart, a law giving kenyan authorities the right to raid newsrooms, listen to journalists' phone calls and control the content of broadcasts on the grounds of "national security". as if these abuses were not enough, the law also provides for huge fines and jail terms for reporters found guilty of "anti-government" practices. although president kibaki ordered the amendment of these provisions a week later, it is not known what these "amendments" are. the law, in its original form, is reminiscent of the dark days of the dictatorship, when the kenyan press was on its knees. kenya is now a democracy, and i am convinced that no one, including president kibaki, wants to go back to those days. an attack on freedom of the press is an attack on democracy. the international community must continue to put pressure on the kenyan authorities to treat civil liberties responsibly and especially press freedom.

madam president, the two important documents we are discussing today – the commission’s plan of action and the report on it – are separated in time by the recent interruption of gas due to the usual winter quarrel between russia and ukraine. consequently, the report is more attuned to reality, trying to increase our internal solidarity and expedite the implementation of the plan in front of us, thus capitalising on the lessons of the last crisis. personally, apart from support for the diversification of transport routes for the import of gas, i consider the appeal to expedite the achievement of internal market energy in the current legislature and the necessity to revisit the entire problem of gas storage as major contributions of the report. however, the recommendation to fully open the nabucco project to russia is questionable since everyone knows that nabucco was conceived as an alternative to russian gas and that, consequently, russia is already doing everything possible to kill it.
the gas crisis we've been facing has manifested itself between ukraine and russia but unfortunately it has affected some of the states of the european union. this crisis has once again demonstrated that the european union is highly dependent on a single gas supply pole. i therefore believe that developing partnerships with russia is beneficial for the whole european union, but at the same time i believe that the european union must immediately start projects to find alternative solutions, precisely in order to prevent the consequences of crises that may occur in the near or distant future. in the same vein, i think we should consider the two projects, nabucco and south stream, as well as other solutions, and here i am referring to the deposits that are at the level of the north sea and those that are supposed to be on the continental shelf of the black sea. since, in time, deposits of all kinds will be exhausted, i believe that we must invest in scientific projects capable of discovering alternative sources of energy, thus ensuring the development of future generations.
the recent gas crisis has brought even more acute attention to the importance of developing alternative energy routes and sources through the development of transport infrastructure and interconnections. in this context, it is necessary to accelerate the nabucco project, which has the potential to contribute to the european union's objectives of diversifying routes, but especially sources of supply from third countries. it is necessary to promote transit with neighbouring countries by completing the projects to interconnect romania with hungary and bulgaria. at the same time, i believe that the south stream project cannot be considered to be in the european interest precisely because it does not use an alternative source, as required by the strategic analysis in the report. but we also have our own energy sources. a micro-hydroelectric plant is not profitable, it is not efficient, but hundreds of thousands of hydroelectric plants from the alps to the carpathians, from the balkans to the tatra or the pyrenees, means energy independence.
in writing. solidarity between the member states of the european union in the field of energy must become a primary objective at european, regional and bilateral levels, and the strategies adopted by each member state at national level must not affect the energy interests of other member states and must correspond to the general interest of the european union in energy security. in this context, the improvement of the community legislative framework on energy interdependence within the eu and the development of a new generation of normative acts aimed at regulating both the european union's relations with non-eu energy suppliers and transit states must serve as an effective instrument in the process of developing european security policy. the new laws will have to provide for legal enforcement mechanisms designed to strengthen energy cooperation and develop viable competition in european energy markets. efforts to increase eu investment in diversifying cross-border structures, stimulating alternative, non-traditional, local energy production and improving infrastructure capacity to facilitate connection to new energy sources should be encouraged. the european union must also take very seriously the need to stimulate the private energy sector in the member states, which is already feeling the effects of the global economic crisis.

in writing. – wilderness can mean different things to different people. i personally perceive wilderness as areas undisturbed by human activities, where natural processes are dominant. so for me, promoting wilderness tourism is a mere contradiction of the term ‘wilderness’. on the other hand, i agree that sustainable tourism, if done properly, can provide an economic incentive for local communities to conserve the natural and cultural heritage. but the increase in demand for wilderness tourism puts pressure on the very same values that the tourists are seeking and can speed up the destruction of fragile ecosystems. a solution would be to open a limited part of wilderness areas to high-quality sustainable tourism, which does not adversely affect the conservation objectives of the sites. tourism activities should be allowed under strict conditions, such as a limited number of tourists per day, and on the basis of a solid sustainable tourism plan that supports conservation initiatives and promotes a responsible experience of wilderness. the tourism plans and the activities of the operators should be evaluated by means of thorough assessment mechanisms, especially designed for wilderness areas. the aim is to make tourists and operators aware that wilderness entails not only freedom but also responsibility.

in writing. gender discrimination is still a reality, unfortunately even in the member states of the european union. this is true not only in the private sector, where men make up nine-tenths of the board of directors of large companies, but also in the public sector, where women are also underrepresented. the lisbon strategy aims to integrate 60% of women who are able to work into the labour market. in addition, it should not be forgotten that one of the major challenges facing europe in the medium and long term is the demographic situation. the european union is experiencing a higher average ageing of its population than other regions of the world, and a population growth of only 0.4%, which means that the european union will have to cope with both a shrinking and an ageing working-age population. it is therefore necessary that the choice between career and raising a family is neither final nor binding, and that these two aspects of life can be balanced.

in writing. at a time when europe is facing a major economic crisis, the final dimensions of which are difficult to estimate, it is expected that the negative effects of labour market movements will be felt by the birth rate, with many women tending not to have a child, afraid of losing their jobs and of the decrease in the material resources needed to care for and educate them. in this context, it is the duty of each member state to promote multi-generational activities, such as 'intergenerational centres', where older people are paid for childcare and education. these intergenerational centres, which are successfully operating in some member states, would allow women who have given birth to a child to return to work quickly and would also facilitate the reintegration of elderly pensioners into the labour market.

in writing. one of the characteristics of child sexual abuse is the rapid growth of the phenomenon via the internet, which makes it increasingly difficult to combat. the blocking of access to child pornography sites must become a legal obligation and the sexual exploitation of children on the internet must be considered a criminal offence. we need to be much more aware of the risk that new technologies will be used by paedophiles, as children increasingly use the internet. we can only worry about the generational gap in terms of internet use and, by implication, the control of children's access to high-risk websites. communication between school and family is very important in preparing children to identify risk situations and react, which is why special information and education programmes, a european strategy to combat sexual abuse and more intensive cooperation between member states are useful in setting up a transnational police network to combat child pornography and prostitution, including a database of perpetrators. from the perspective of european cooperation, the slowness with which the 2007 council of europe convention is being ratified is regrettable.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the niebler report because cooperation between the eu and russia in the field of science and technology is necessary. the eu-russia agreement should stimulate both the european community and russia to gain mutual benefits from scientific and technical progress achieved through research programmes. the agreement will allow the exchange of ideas and the transfer of know-how to the benefit of the scientific community, industry and citizens. i note that this agreement is based on similar principles to the one concluded between the eu and the usa in the same scientific and technological field. it should be noted that the agreement is based on the principles of mutual benefit, promotes participation in cooperation activities such as 'coordinated calls for proposals for joint projects, access to each other's programmes and activities'. the principles of effective protection of intellectual property and fair sharing of intellectual property rights shall be promoted. the proposal also provides for missions of eu experts and officials, workshops, seminars and meetings to be organised in the european community and in russia. in the european year of creativity and innovation, we hope that this agreement will help to make the eu-russia strategic partnership more effective.
in writing. − the renewal of the partnership agreement for scientific and technological cooperation with russia is an important step in normalising and strengthening relations between the eu and the russian federation, beyond the tensions of the recent period. however, the normality of collaborative relations in these areas is not sufficient. the eu and russia must first find a way to strengthen partnership and cooperation in security policies and, above all, in energy security policy. the recent gas crisis has shown us the need to deal seriously and unitedly with the problem of the european union's dependence on its suppliers of resources. let us also not forget the crisis in georgia which, for a time, threatened the entire post-cold war european architecture. in the face of all the challenges of globalisation and the global crisis, russia is an important player that cannot be excluded or ignored from the negotiating table. but the russian federation must abide by these agreements as well as the normal international rules. i call on the ec and the czech presidency to find concrete ways of resolving these problems as soon as possible, for the benefit of both themselves and european citizens, as well as the partner third countries (ukraine, the republic of moldova).

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank you for this debate. i believe it was very useful. if you had listened to the debate in the last council meeting during lunch, you would have seen a similar will to cope with the problem, but also an appreciation of the complexity of the problem we are discussing. it has a moral and political dimension, but also a security and legal dimension. we all agree that president obama’s decision to close guantánamo was an important and good one, which we all appreciate and which is applauded by practically all of you here. but now that we are discussing the consequences and what we can do to express solidarity – and our interest here is to act in transatlantic harmony – we of course see that the problem is a complex one. martin schulz has said that we cannot fight terrorism and at the same time get into a conflict over fundamental rights. he is perfectly right, but hartmut nassauer has said that there are two dimensions: one is the moral one and the other concerns security. he is also right, and that is exactly why the ministers of justice and home affairs have to discuss this as well. from the political perspective, it is not just a flexing of moral muscles, nor should we approach this problem just out of guilt. it is certainly more complex than that. graham watson spoke of the need to approach this with one voice. again, he is certainly right, but at the same time – because this also concerns the legal problem and the competence issue – we cannot force the member states to invite the detainees from guantánamo on demand. if you had to solve this problem by deciding to invite those detainees to your homes – imagine taking on the responsibility of the ministers of the interior – you would certainly think twice about how this problem is to be handled. i certainly do not think it should be approached by the council and the member states as an issue of horse-trading – not at all. it is not about washing ourselves but not getting wet. at the core of the problem is simply the fact that the decision to close guantánamo is, of course, the primary responsibility of the united states, the country which built the facility. but we have – and have to have – the goodwill to express solidarity and to be cooperative in solving the problem. there is also the tactical debate. should we offer this on a gold plate now, or should we wait until a request has been made? but if we do receive a request, we need to be prepared to react. therefore the council started to discuss this seriously on the second day after president obama’s decision. i do not think we can underestimate the security issue – as you have pointed out – as it is a simple fact that some of the inmates who were released re-engaged in terrorist activity, and it is a simple matter of fact that one man, mr said al-shihri, is now the deputy head of al-qa’ida in yemen. so the us has to start the serious work of clearing up who those people are, and we have to break with them. legally, i think we have to be aware that the decision on the admission of foreign nationals to eu member states is the national competence of the member states. this is one level. however, on a second level, there is the agreement that we should now work towards a european framework in which to embed the national decision. both the schengen and the dublin agreements call for a european approach because the security of all schengen members will be affected in some way by the decision of the individual member states. so there is an internal imperative for a coordinated approach. furthermore, the eu is looking into the possibility of assisting the us with the resettlement and rehabilitation of former detainees in third countries. some of you have raised the question of speed: can we act faster than we are doing now? i think we should be aware that the discussion has only just begun. it has only been one week. the questions that have to be addressed are really complex and will need some time, although president obama himself has requested a review of the prisoners’ files and has set a one-year deadline for the closure of guantánamo. one should not expect the council to be ready to fix all these complex problems in a matter of a few days. furthermore, it has to be kept in mind that the primary responsibility for the guantánamo rests with the us. although the member states express their readiness to work on a coordinated approach, the issue has a bilateral dimension as well as the multilateral one. a clear position of the respective member states on the resettlement of detainees is not yet known. the meeting of the justice and home affairs ministers which is to take place later this month will be very useful here. in the meantime, the anti-terrorist coordinator, gilles de kerchove, is also working on various option papers here. so that is my summary on guantánamo, which occupied most of the time. on the other issue of illegal detention, mr fava’s favourite issue, i will just repeat what has been said several times by my predecessors: the allegation concerned the involvement of national intelligence agencies; the supervision of those agencies is the responsibility of individual member states, and the council has no power here to act beyond what was done.
the commission's vice-president - mr president, the commission broadly shares the views expressed by the president-in-office of the council, mr vondra. i would like to say, however, that we are at a turning point in this long debate. this is a fundamental turning point in the fight against terrorism: we must now try to engage in this fight with a restored moral authority for the entire western community, a fight in respect of fundamental values and fundamental rights. europe must also involve the entire international community in this desire to fight terrorism from now on, bearing in mind the fundamental values which are the very motives behind this fight. this is a crucial turning point and parliament's declaration is extremely useful in this respect because it presupposes a willingness on the part of all the member states to participate in this major change. it is true, however, that the united states has the primary responsibility. the united states must be prepared to verify the status of each detainee before making a formal request to us for transfer to a member state of the union. it is indeed the indispensable condition. the united states must make a clear and reasoned request on a case-by-case basis. this is absolutely essential. it is true that it is up to each member state to decide in the end whether or not to accept a former guantanamo detainee, but the debate has shown that consultation at european level is obviously very, very desirable. coordination will be beneficial in determining the legal status of former detainees. it will also be necessary to protect member states against diplomatic or other requests from the country of origin of such detainees. it will be necessary to reassure the member states, in particular - i am thinking of what mr nassauer told us - those who have a concern about public order and security. the coordinated european approach will also improve the bargaining power vis-à-vis the united states on access to documents and on the modalities of transfer, and we may then be able to add financial aid to facilitate this reception in certain member states. i say this in front of mr vondra: we will of course work closely with the czech presidency. we are in fact drafting with mr de kerchove the reflection paper which will serve as a basis for the discussion which will take place at the jha council on 26 february. and then, i can say here, we will probably take the opportunity of our visit to washington with mr langer, who is the president of the council of ministers of the interior, to raise with the american interlocutors all the questions surrounding these problems relating to and following the closure of guantánamo. we must now deal with this matter very seriously and prepare ourselves legally to respond to the american demand on a case-by-case basis. this must be done very, very seriously, while of course taking into account the desire for positive cooperation in this new fight against terrorism, which is in fact based on adherence to the true fundamental values that unite us and that must unite the entire world community. thank you, everybody.
