on behalf of the pse group. i would first like to congratulate my colleague el khadraoui and mr jarzembowski. the transport sector is one of the key sectors for the economic and social development of the european union. at the request of the european parliament, the european commission has proposed the internalisation of external costs and the amendment of the eurovignette directive. the timing is, however, extremely difficult. the economic crisis is causing orders to drop, freight forwarders to have high costs, businesses to close and jobs to be lost. the commission's proposed texts are a step forward in the development of transport that respects and protects the environment, but they can and must be improved. i do not think that mr jarzembowski's approach, in which we only criticize without improving, is the right one. i personally believe that a directive which is not binding on all member states will not achieve its aim and can significantly distort the internal market by the barriers which some member states, if they wish, can introduce to the free movement of persons and goods. i therefore believe that the internalisation of external costs should apply to all types of transport and that double taxation should be avoided. thus, if some member states have decided to introduce a road fee, then they should no longer introduce an additional pollution fee. this is also the position of mr el khadraoui, which i support. the cost of congestion is 1% of gross domestic product. we must therefore act to reduce it, but the cost of these measures is not to be borne only by road hauliers and road hauliers. congestion is due to all vehicles and, in particular, to a poor infrastructure. member states must invest in the construction of motorways, high-speed railways and other alternatives that can reduce congestion. co-modality will enable the transfer of goods from the road system to the rail, sea or air system and will make the transport of goods and people more efficient. in conclusion, we need an integrated strategy for the development of european transport, with environmental protection, but without the internalisation of external costs affecting the competitiveness of road transport.
a coherent and sustainable european transport policy is needed, respecting the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. internalising the external costs of pollution and noise is a positive measure. fees for heavy-duty road infrastructure use will in the long term support the massive infrastructure investments included in the european and national economic recovery plans, both at the level of trans-european transport networks and at the level of other categories of road infrastructure, including in mountain areas where road construction is often particularly arduous. in the short term, however, it is up to the member states to find concrete and rapid ways of financing these investments through the judicious use of the funds made available by the union, both through the ten-t financial framework and through the structural and cohesion funds, as well as through concessions and public-private partnerships. the european commission must support, through the instruments at its disposal, the integrated infrastructure network extension initiatives of the member states, especially the new member states. as regards the introduction of a charge for infrastructure users to solve the congestion problem, i believe that this proposal should be studied further, given that it does not depend exclusively on motor vehicles, but more particularly on the ability of member states to plan and implement their territorial infrastructure efficiently at regional and local level. for this reason, i believe that there is a need for better coordination between spatial planning, urban planning and traffic management, particularly in urban and peri-urban areas, where congestion is the most common problem.
the commission's desire to charge transport operators not only for the right to use the infrastructure but also for environmental effects, the so-called internalisation of external costs, will represent a tax burden with severe consequences for the companies concerned, especially in the context of the current economic crisis. before such a directive is put forward, concrete impact studies based on relevant statistical data are needed; a realistic estimate of the consequences of applying such a directive is needed and concrete proposals are needed on the methods of calculating and accounting for external costs. internalising the external costs of transport is, in the long term, a measure that can help to greenerise transport and i note that such concrete legislative instruments are indeed needed in member states such as romania. however, i do not see a future application of these external costs, at least not in my home city of bucharest. i am talking about traffic congestion, air pollution, noise pollution, water pollution, soil pollution or damage to natural landscapes. i find it hard to believe that the romanian authorities will implement this directive which is more burdensome than helpful. however, as mr jarzembowski points out, the application of such measures must be the result of objective studies based on statistical data; we cannot ask transport companies to pay arbitrarily fixed amounts for external costs, especially since these amounts are significant.

i want to congratulate you on what you're doing for children and the internet and also on your decision to have 100% broadband coverage by the year 2010. i mean, in romania, the elderly, parents communicate cheaply and effectively with children who are abroad via the internet; they see and hear them. however, i want to ask you what you are doing for the development of electronic services. i'm talking about the public key infrastructure.
the czech presidency was right: the barcelona objectives were set before the last enlargement. but he was fundamentally wrong in claiming that the specificity of the new states and their previous experience would be arguments against these objectives. on the contrary, the benefits are important: for parents and gender equality, for the economy and employment, for children and the future. the relatively low wages in our countries force both parents to work; it is not an option, it is a necessity. single-parent families are also on the rise, with nearly a third of children in some countries born outside the traditional family. policies that encourage labour mobility, seen as a factor of efficiency, cannot always ignore the fact that people have children. many of them live in poor families, without adequate food, health, and education. sometimes the environment is violent. by going to work, they're also left alone. these services can break the chain of poverty and provide a positive alternative to socialising under the guidance of a specialist staff. but to fulfil this role, day-care centres must be: 1. available, but above all accessible, free of charge or at affordable costs; and 2. of good quality. here, the professionalism of the staff is essential. to combat the crisis, we are selling off nearly new cars to buy new ones, wasting valuable material resources. it is preferable to invest in the construction of nurseries and kindergartens and to create stable jobs for those who work in this field. the quality of human resources has long been a criterion for distinguishing between nations. we propose that the commission take public expenditure per child seriously in evaluating employment programmes in each state. it is true that jacques delors once said that every child is a treasure and that it is the task of society to discover it. but i would add this: if we do not, society is undermining its future as a whole.
according to the european commission's october 2008 report on the implementation of the barcelona objectives on pre-school childcare facilities, member states have not met the targets set by eu leaders. in this context, i recommend the following actions: 1. increasing the involvement of national governments in this issue;2. creating a body of specialists at national government level to deal strictly with this issue only; 3. the development of eu control over member state governments through a set of specific instruments. all these measures would help to ensure equal opportunities for women and men, improve the quality of life and offset demographic ageing by boosting the birth rate.
the country i represent has long been on the list of those who do not have a social policy for childcare that meets european standards. gradually, things improved, with qualitative methods being adopted as a result of the specialization of the care staff. the barcelona objectives have motivated institutions that aim at child protection and care standards have brought responsibilities and competences, and children enjoy humane treatment. now that the birth rate is falling, we must give equal opportunities to those with special social status, and both the member states and the european commission must make efforts to educate them, and then to integrate them into society. they have inferiority complexes toward other home-grown children; hence, programs that allow them to spend time with family and socialize could help these children to regain their social standing.
women's involvement in work, politics and encouragement to take on more responsibilities depends on the availability of childcare facilities. women need to be encouraged to plan for their careers, and this cannot be done without an effective system for childcare. every euro invested in childcare facilities is a benefit of between six and nine euros for society, through the creation of jobs and better educational conditions. the fact that in many european member states you have to register for example in daycare, just before the baby is born, or that there are queues of several months to register for kindergarten, shows that childcare facilities in europe are not sufficient. child care facilities not only help women advance their careers, but most importantly, they develop the children's skills as members of society. i also want to say that in this time of crisis it's important to invest in education, health, to invest practically in the future.
substitute for the author. - i would first like to thank my colleagues in the committee on employment and social affairs, the esp secretariat within the commission for promoting this subject on migrant children, which we are debating today in plenary, because when we talk about children, we are talking about our future, about the future of the european union. labour migration is a growing phenomenon internationally, but also within the union. migration has great potential for development, but it also presents serious challenges, both in the developed and the least developed countries of the european union. we can talk about the positive impact of migration on the economy of migrant workers' countries of origin, because it can reduce poverty and increase investment in human capital, but the situation of migrant children, who are left alone in their country of origin when their parents emigrate in search of work in another country, is an issue that has caused concern in some member states over the last two years. although there are comprehensive policies to improve the lives and education of migrant children who have moved abroad with their parents, the phenomenon of children left at home has received less attention. parental emigration is a complex social phenomenon with a complex impact on the dynamics and functioning of the family, but also on society as a whole. children of migrant workers are a vulnerable group at risk. the complexity of the phenomenon, its causes and consequences, the dynamics and how legislation is effectively implemented on the ground, and the practices of professionals, have posed many challenges not only for the authorities but also for civil society. in this context, romanian civil society and media have presented studies that mention that in romania there are over 350 000 children whose parents work abroad, of which 126 000 children have both parents gone. the negative consequences of parental absence are felt by children primarily on a psychological level.feeling depressed, lack of interest in school and extracurricular activities can be direct consequences of parental absence. a direct consequence of parental migration is the deprivation of the child of parental affection and supervision necessary for normal development. in the absence of parents and the care of children by persons unable to provide emotional and educational support, these two consequences can in turn have negative effects on the health and psychological development of children, their involvement in deviant or age-inappropriate behaviour and their exposure to other forms of exploitation or abuse. as a mother and a european social democrat, i am advocating for the respect of the rights of all children, their equal opportunities, the role of the state and investment in the training of the new generations. identifying the most vulnerable, excluded or marginalised children should be the focus of any research effort, thus ensuring that appropriate leverage is created to support the efforts of authorities to ensure the rights of all children. commissioner špidla, i would like to thank you very much for the contribution you made by transmitting the video message to the european conference on children left at home that i organised in bucharest last november. given the complexity of this phenomenon, especially in the context of the current economic and social crisis, which primarily affects vulnerable groups, including children, i would like to ask you, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, whether the commission intends to carry out a study to assess the extent of the situation and whether the commission considers that the issue of migrant workers' children is a problem only for the government of the country of origin or also for the governments of the host countries which benefit from the presence of migrants on the labour market.
according to a study by unicef and the association alternative sociale, in romania, for approximately 350 000 children, one of the parents works abroad, and for 126 000 both parents. these results are worrying. i believe that the following measures could improve this situation: 1. the national governments of migrant origin, together with the governments of labour-absorbing countries, together with the european commission, to create a joint programme through which migrant workers will have access to specific childcare services, the school and educational system, and language courses, services accessible to all segments of migrant workers; 2.the commission, together with the governments of the employing states, should develop a strategy to provide certain facilities to employers so that they can offer employees and a package of specific services through which migrant workers can take their children to the countries where they work. i believe that these measures would be conducive to the harmonious development and upbringing of these children, since they too represent the future of europe.
i would like to stress one thing: the flow of labour we are talking about is from the less developed countries to the more developed countries of the union. the possibility of entering the labour markets of developed countries is usually considered a great advantage offered, and the high amounts entering the countries of origin are constantly brought up as an argument. the facts here show another side of the story: in addition to lower labor costs, developed countries are outsourcing some of the labor costs. they remain the responsibility of the communities and states where the workers come from and are significant. in this context, cohesion policies and solidarity between member states should not be seen as a kind of altruism of the rich towards the poor. these are absolutely necessary policies, acts of justice, if the european union is to remain consistent with its values and maintain the attachment of its citizens to those values.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, before i address the subject of our debate today, let me start by expressing my deep condolences to relatives of the victims in the tragic incident in baden-württemberg today. now let me turn to the subject of our debate today. firstly, we are grateful for the opportunity to have this debate. this is an important issue, as you all know well. a number of operational difficulties have led to specific problems in getting sis ii up and running. the presidency wishes, as you request, to be completely transparent with you about the history of and the background on this issue. because of the negative results of the original tests on the system, further tests were conducted in november and december 2008. the final results of these operational system tests were only known in the second half of january 2009. at their informal meeting of 15 january 2009 in prague, justice and home affairs ministers were informed by the commission that the outcome of these tests had been less than satisfactory. the ministers agreed immediately on the need to implement a new global sis ii management approach, involving member states working together with the commission. the new management approach will provide for closer monitoring of the project, thereby allowing for early warning of any potential difficulties. it was also agreed that measures would be taken at a subsequent jha council, which took place on 26 and 27 february 2009. at that meeting, the council agreed in its conclusion to invite the commission to keep parliament and the presidency of the council fully informed about problems related to sis ii and the way forward. this parliament has asked whether the problems identified to date will require the system to be rebuilt. according to the information received by the council on the status of the sis ii project, a number of problems persist. however, we understand that the view of the commission is that all outstanding issues can be resolved without a major redesign of the sis ii application. at its february meeting, the council endorsed the implementation of the sis ii analysis and repair plan, which will allow for the identification of all issues and their immediate solution, as well as the evaluation of the technical architecture so as to ensure a stable and flawless sis ii system. nevertheless, the council also agreed that the contingency plan should be followed in case serious problems emerge which could not be resolved. as far as an alternative to sis ii is concerned, the jha council in february welcomed the completion of the feasibility study serving as a basis for creating a workable, alternative technical scenario for developing sis ii based on sis i+ evolution as a part of the contingency plan. the council also requested that as soon as possible, and by may 2009 at the latest, a report containing an in-depth assessment and comparison of both scenarios should be submitted to the council by the presidency and the commission. the council will assess, on the basis of this report, the progress made on sis ii development and, as far as the alternative scenario is concerned, will examine the prospect of achieving the objective of sis ii as set out in the legal framework governing the establishment, operation and use of sis ii, on the technical basis of sis i+ evolution. this examination will be carried out as soon as possible and at the latest by the council meeting on 4 and 5 june 2009. as to the details requested by parliament on the resolution of the outstanding problems and in particular the financial aspects, the council invited the commission not only to inform the european parliament about the problems related to sis ii, but also to inform both parliament and the council fully and on a regular basis about the expenditure figures related to the central sis ii project and to measures taken to ensure complete financial transparency. on the basis of the report requested from the presidency and commission, the council will, at the latest by its meeting in june 2009, discuss the calendar for entry into operation of sis ii. this will take into account the provisions on time schedules set out in parliament’s resolution of 24 september 2008 on the draft council regulation on immigration from the schengen information system – sis i+ – to the second-generation schengen information system – sis ii. this was incorporated into article 19 of the council regulation of 24 october. i am sure that the commission will be able to provide some additional information in response to the questions raised. i would simply like to assure you, the members of this parliament, that the presidency will follow this issue closely and ensure that the way forward agreed last the commission's vice-president - mr president, i would like to confirm what minister vondra said. i should also like to say that together with mr langer, the president of the council of ministers for home affairs, we have made the problem of sis ii a top priority. i shall try to give you some details. the commission's main contractor for the development of sis ii has carried out an operational test campaign on the central system interacting with a number of national systems. between november and december 2008, the results of these tests led us to conclude that the central system had not reached the contractual level. as early as mid-november, the commission launched an in-depth analysis exercise of the sis ii solution, currently being developed by hewlett-packard/steria, in collaboration with member states' experts and with the help and assistance of two renowned it consultancy firms. following the failure of the operational tests, we have therefore implemented an analysis and repair plan estimated to last four months. the objective of this plan is to bring the application and implementation of sis ii to a satisfactory level of stability and performance. the plan aims, firstly, to fix known bugs related to the central system a number of bugs have already been fixed and, secondly, to verify that the application, implementation of sis ii is not affected by insurmountable structural weaknesses. targeted testing is being carried out in a number of priority areas to remove uncertainties in the architecture of the current solution, this activity being carried out in parallel with the finalisation of the technical analysis of the fundamental problems. on the other hand, the commission has put in place a global approach to project management to better integrate the central and national components of sis ii, while respecting the legally established competences of the commission and the member states. in concrete terms, the commission is coordinating a common project management structure. this common management structure brings together the national project managers, the central project managers and the commission's contractors. this structure will accompany the project throughout the analysis and repair period, then during the qualification tests, then during the migration phase, until the start of sis ii. at the end of the analysis and repair period we will have a clear idea of the means still to be used to start up sis ii and the corresponding timetable, as vice-premier vondra has just said. the objective of putting sis ii into operation in september 2009 will undoubtedly be delayed. the current difficulties of the sis ii project were discussed at the informal ministerial meeting on 15 january and at the justice and home affairs council on 26 and 27 february. the broad lines of the approach advocated by the commission for the continuation of the sis ii project were accepted. first, the need to continue the analysis of the feasibility of an alternative technical solution based on the current sis i+ was supported by the council. we are therefore in a position to continue this feasibility analysis of an alternative solution. but any alternative technical solution will of course have to be in accordance with the legal framework for sis ii as adopted by you and the council. of course, great care will have to be taken to ensure maximum reuse of investments and to the situation of the member states and associated countries which intend to join the schengen area in the coming years. the ministers agreed to meet, as has just been said, in june at the latest - early june - to take stock of the progress made and, if necessary, to define new guidelines and, if necessary, to switch to an alternative option. with this in mind, the council requested that, as soon as possible and no later than may 2009, the presidency and the commission, in close cooperation with the sis ii task force and in consultation with the appropriate bodies, present to the council a report containing a detailed assessment and comparison of the two scenarios. to this end, common criteria for comparison were agreed to assess the respective merits and disadvantages of each solution. clearly, this means that we will indeed have a council decision at the beginning of june, in the light of all the tests that have been carried out, and this will allow, we believe, to continue with sis ii or, possibly, to move towards an alternative solution but which will of course remain in line with the objectives you have defined. i was of course very sensitive to what mr coelho and mrs roure said, namely the need for greater transparency. i would like to say that we will send and will continue to send reports in writing. i believe that the project to improve the european union's external border management mechanism should not be seen as an attempt to stop migration as a process. the real purpose of eu border security measures is not necessarily to stem immigration flows, but to control them closely. the right management of migration is a positive factor for the societies and economies of the eu member states. i would like to stress that the european union should pay more attention to the management of its peripheral borders where there are conflict zones. the work carried out so far by the european union border assistance mission between the republic of moldova and ukraine (eubam) is highly commendable, characterised by the establishment of a single customs regime at the border, the creation of barriers to smuggling and the reduction of the activity of criminal groups. on the other hand, the ongoing unresolved transnistrian conflict makes it quite difficult for the moldovan authorities to manage this border segment, where a large flow of illegal migration continues to persist. i would like to express my conviction that the european union has sufficient political, economic and security leverage to curb the above-mentioned illegal actions, including to become more actively involved in resolving the frozen conflicts on its eastern peripheries.

president-in-office of the council. − madam president, i think this debate is a timely one and that mrs neyts-uyttebroeck’s report includes a number of important recommendations. it gives me the opportunity to raise an issue which is central to our policy towards the western balkans. the work of the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia (icty) is an essential element in rendering justice, coming to terms with the past and moving forward. it is also key to strengthening the rule of law in the region. this can be a slow, and at times difficult, process, but the icty has made important progress. so far it has completed proceedings against 116 accused with very different verdicts. only two of 161 indictees remain at large. when the icty was set up in 1993 the domestic judicial systems in the former yugoslavia were unprepared for dealing with crimes of this scale. yet it was clear that they had to be addressed. no contract, no agreement, no society can be sustainable without justice. our strategy towards the region is to assist in stabilising the countries of the western balkans and helping them realise their eu perspective. a central element of that policy is cooperation with the icty. we support its mandate in several ways. firstly, the countries of the western balkans are part of the stabilisation and association process (sap). this process depends on respect for democratic principles, the rule of law, human rights and the rights of persons belonging to minorities, fundamental freedoms and the principles of international law and regional cooperation. it also depends on full cooperation with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia. sap conditionality is monitored through the annual progress reports prepared by the commission. the next progress reports will be published in october 2009. in addition, human rights and rule-of-law issues, including strengthening the functioning, impartiality and responsibility of the judiciary system, and the fight against corruption and organised crime are key priorities of the eu’s european partnership with the countries of the western balkans. these are updated on a regular basis. furthermore, the council has adopted two common positions aimed at supporting the implementation of the mandate of the icty by imposing an assets freeze on indicted fugitives and a travel ban on persons assisting icty indictees to evade justice. these common positions are regularly extended and updated. the european union will support the work of the icty until it has been completed. i entirely agree that in the longer term the legacy of the icty must be preserved. whenever this happens – and it is not a matter for the eu to decide – the domestic judicial systems will need to be ready to take over the icty’s files. this is one of the reasons why the emphasis we have placed on judicial reform and good governance in the sap is so important. the work of ngos and individuals, such as the humanitarian law centre in belgrade and the research and documentation centre in sarajevo, who are seeking after the truth, also deserves our full support. let me close by thanking this parliament for your support in this area and in particular for this helpful and constructive report.

mr president, the eastern partnership is a project which covers six countries. one of them, belarus, is a dramatic example of self-isolation, to which we have responded in the past with a policy marked by the ‘too little, too late’ syndrome, both in terms of sanctions and of incentives. belarus has little in common with, say, georgia. cooperation between mr lukashenko and mr saakashvili looks like political fiction and political horror combined. the other five countries are on the black sea, where we have a synergy – which means that there is no strategy yet. could the eastern partnership stand in for a black sea strategy? one could hardly imagine a regional strategy there without turkey and russia, but these particular countries are left out of the process. what all these countries have in common is the fact that they were all part of the soviet union, and they are all neighbours of russia as much as they are neighbours of the european union. in other words, we are dealing with a common neighbourhood. russia looks to that neighbourhood as being its reserved sphere of interest. we certainly cannot accept that but, on the other hand, the eastern partnership appears to be a way to reciprocate the russian policy on its neighbourhood. this makes that neighbourhood an area of conflicting interests and rivalry. the real challenge is how to develop an eu-russia common policy in respect of their common neighbourhood. otherwise we will not achieve security and stability there, but the opposite. as far as everything else is concerned, we already have democracy and good governance, economic integration and convergence, energy security and human contacts on the agenda. from this point of view, ukraine is much further advanced than the others, and i assume that it is not very happy to see that our offer now has to be shared with the others. the real problem was not the lack of labels but the lack of delivery. by putting our money where our mouth is – and of course, madam commissioner, you are perfectly right to say that we need a budget in order to make good policy – and by adding a little visionary realism instead of naive confrontation, we might really transform the eastern partnership into a valuable and positive asset.
the eastern partnership initiative is of particular importance and a set of tools to facilitate its implementation needs to be implemented as soon as possible. i welcome the collaborative platform promoted by this new partnership framework, because the need to recalibrate the relationship with our neighbours is vital, not only to make our cooperation with them more efficient, but also to be able to solve the major problems we face today - the economic crisis, energy security - which cannot be managed exclusively at the domestic level. the partnership shall stimulate projects of the utmost importance to the union by promoting an institutionalised framework that places both the relationship with neighbours and intra-regional cooperation in the neighbourhood at a higher level. there are priority projects that are indispensable to tackling the energy crisis: those in the black sea region and those using resources in the caspian sea area. they can only be implemented in a secure neighbourhood and close relationship with relevant regional actors, based on mutually beneficial joint commitments.
mr president, my speech looks at the relationship between the eastern partnership and the black sea synergy. in my opinion, the main obstacle is finding the synergy’s proper place in this increasingly complex picture of eu initiatives towards the east. consequently, the real substantive issues of the black sea area, like energy and frozen conflicts, are approached either through: the eu neighbourhood policy, where the money is; the future eastern partnership, designed to increase the security confidence of the countries involved and secure the energy deliveries to the eu after the georgian war; the eu’s strategic relationship with russia and ukraine; or the accession talks with turkey. what then, is, left for the black sea synergy to achieve? not much, i should say, apart from seminars and studies on how to extend the existing european initiatives towards the area and non-political issues. it is, therefore, necessary to improve the substance, too, of the framework known as ‘synergy’ if one wants to maintain its credibility.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs roth-behrendt, and her two shadow rapporteurs, mrs ries and mrs grossetête, very warmly for the constructive and intensive cooperation which helped us to reach an agreement at first reading. it is a regulation which has three important results, three important advances: we are creating more security, we are creating more transparency for consumers and we are achieving a substantial simplification of existing legislation. we have all seen the focus of our work, particularly in the area of security. i would just like to make a few points. we are actually creating for the first time a real mechanism which i would like to call 'cosmetic surveillance', i.e. a constant monitoring of cosmetic products - something we already have in pharmaceutical products. we are intensifying market surveillance by the member states, and we are introducing mandatory traceability of cosmetic products. all these things apply to all producers, from the amateur to the wholesaler and retailer, that is to say to all the actors in the entire distribution chain. mrs roth-behrendt has already said something on the subject of nanomaterials. we have found a solution here which i would call model-like, because the same solution will be used again later this week in another important piece of legislation. the specific provisions on nanomaterials used in cosmetics provide for a mechanism for such information before the materials are placed on the market in the community. this ensures that relevant safety data are submitted and that the authorities have time to take any necessary safety precautions. there has been a long, very intensive and fruitful debate on whether substances classified as carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction may be used in exceptional circumstances. i am very pleased that the council and parliament have agreed with the commission that we should stick to the general ban on these substances in cosmetics. the minimum exceptions proposed by the commission are only intended to avoid any inconsistency with food law, because it is not immediately obvious that alcohol may be drunk but not used in cosmetics. in addition to product safety, the proposal will improve consumer information. among other things, the list of ingredients shall indicate which substances are contained in nanoform. in addition, instruments are provided for the purposeful verification of the manufacturer's information. i am happy to confirm that the member states and the commission want to prevent the possibility of misleading consumers by working closely together on this issue. i said that this regulation is also part of our simplification programme. this is the removal of ambiguities and contradictions from a directive that is already 33 years old and has been amended 55 times since then. i don't think anyone could really understand her anymore. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would also point out that the creation of a central system for the notification of cosmetic products before they are placed on the community market will bring cost savings for the industry. i have already mentioned that parliament, the council and the commission have worked together closely and constructively. i can agree with all the amendments tabled by the rapporteur, mrs roth-behrendt, on behalf of the commission. the commission is also giving all the explanations requested by parliament on the question of a regulation instead of a directive, on the question of internet sales, on the question of counterfeiting of products, on the question of transitional provisions and the timeframe for the application of the regulation and on the question of the definition of nanomaterials. in order to save time, i would ask you to agree to these statements being sent to the chambers, since the content of them is already known to parliament. commission statementsthe commission takes note of the concerns of member states on the recasting of directives into regulations. the commission considers that where the existing provisions of a directive are sufficiently clear, precise and detailed, they may be capable of conversion into directly applicable provisions in a regulation by way of recasting. this is true more particularly where the provisions in question are of a technical nature and have already been fully transposed into national law by all member states. the commission accepts, in the light of the different opinions expressed, that the specific case of the cosmetics regulation will not be used as a precedent for the interpretation of the interinstitutional agreement on this point. the commission commits to clarifying the situation regarding internet sales of cosmetic products prior to the date of application of the regulation. like the european parliament, the commission is concerned that the cosmetics sector may be affected by counterfeiting which may increase risk for human health. therefore, the commission will take action in order to enhance cooperation between national competent authorities in order to fight counterfeiting. the commission will draft an explanatory note concerning transitional provisions and dates of application of the regulation (in particular in view of articles 7, 8, 10 and 12a). the commission notes that work towards a common definition of nanomaterials is still evolving. the commission therefore confirms that in future community legislation progress on the common definition should be taken into account and notes that the comitology procedures contained in this proposal also allow for the updating of the definition in this proposal.
on behalf of the pse group. cosmetics are certainly of great importance to european consumers and should therefore be given due attention. it considers it appropriate to initiate a review of the directive and replace it with a proposal for a regulation from the commission. this will remove legal inaccuracies and inconsistencies and avoid differences between transpositions into national legislation. as experience at european level has shown that the 'ingredient by ingredient' approach is neither viable nor sufficient, i believe that greater responsibility for producers and rigorous control of the internal market are our priorities. the use of nanomaterials is a promising solution in this area, with the intention that they will be evaluated and declared safe by the scientific committee for consumer products, while the use of alternative methods is an initiative that needs to be further supported. i believe that the involvement of the committee to which i referred is essential, as regards the use of substances classified as carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic, to verify their use in the manufacture of cosmetic products. for the effective implementation of this regulation, i believe it is necessary for member states to carry out appropriate checks and, in the event of non-compliance, to report regularly to the commission.

in writing. food prices have risen sharply recently. there are two reasons for this: on the one hand, the world food and agricultural crisis, and on the other, the concentration of the retail market, which has risen from 21.7% in 1990 to over 70% today. consumer prices are on average five times higher than those of the producer. supermarket chains often impose unfair conditions and make it difficult for farmers and small suppliers to access the market. i support the idea of the european commission to create a european market monitoring system. i support the idea of a european competition network. funds from the rural development programme should have higher allocations in favour of producers. the idea of revitalizing the concept of 'local produce', more effectively supporting traditional food markets are solutions that i strongly support.
in writing. i welcome the batzeli report which highlights the wide differences between the prices of agri-food products in supermarkets and those charged to producers. this is unfortunately also the case in countries with a standard of living well below the european average, such as romania. if we reject any proposal for price controls, we cannot but note that the bargaining power of supermarkets is excessive in relation to producers. and here we can act more firmly in the framework of competition and consumer protection policy.
in writing. the approach of the european parliament elections brings to the fore, as always, the problem of the lack of information and dialogue with citizens, which is specific to the european area. in this context, i welcome the motion for a resolution on active dialogue with citizens, which stresses the importance of involving the european institutions, the trans-european education system and the media. the rejection of the constitutional treaty in france and the netherlands and the opposition to the lisbon treaty by referendum in ireland have shown that action by citizens with a low level of education is a viable and necessary strategy, which i fully support. given the high level of internet access in the member states of the european union, we should take advantage of this tool and use it to make the dialogue with citizens more effective. in this way, opinions could be recorded, which would then be evaluated and incorporated into our decision-making process. i also believe that the history and functioning of the union and the rights of citizens should be core components of the european curriculum. in this way, i am convinced, the premises can be secured for a coherent dialogue with citizens, who will approach europe and the european union from a different perspective, based on accurate information and knowledge.
in writing. the linguistic and cultural diversity of the union of 27 european states is an asset for understanding and cooperation, for cross-border labour mobility and for the assimilation of european values. it is important to continuously improve eu policies to encourage mother tongue education and to guarantee mutual interlingual intelligibility. we need cooperation between national authorities and the european commission to implement the most effective practices for integration by accepting linguistic differences. romania is one of the eu countries that provides a degree of protection and support above the european average for minorities, encouraging education in their own languages. the 'babes-bolyai' university in cluj-napoca is a shining example of promoting multilingualism. unfortunately, even at the european parliament, demonstrations were organized and initiatives were launched that, in the name of false discrimination, demanded the destruction of the university of "babes-bolyai" on the basis of separation on ethnic grounds. that is why i want to draw attention to the danger of exacerbating ethnic discourse. respect for minority rights and the promotion of multilingualism must not be perverted into a screen behind which work is done against the european spirit and interethnic harmony. multilingualism must be a common denominator, not a factor of division in the european union.
in writing. there are pragmatic arguments in favour of multilingualism: it reduces the risk of unemployment, increases the chances of employment, allows for an increase in the quality of services provided and labour productivity, facilitates mobility. we all know them; opinions converge on this point. i would like to emphasise here the importance of another reason for supporting multilingualism and related measures. multilingualism helps to affirm values and attitudes that are essential to the european social model: mutual understanding, trust and solidarity; it can help to achieve unity in a diverse world. to this end, we also insist on the need to preserve europe's linguistic diversity. one way to achieve this would be to learn, as a second foreign language, languages other than those of universal circulation. they can learn languages of their neighbours, of ethnic minorities in their own country, languages spoken in emerging economies with which relations are developing. i am confident that the positive effects of such a policy will be felt in everyday life.
in writing. i congratulate my colleague, mr graça moura, on the way in which he has succeeded in combining the general, regional and local interests in this draft report. personally, i have proposed that citizens who belong to an ethnic group speaking a minority language should thoroughly learn the official language of the state of residence. this would certainly be an advantage in finding a job and in ensuring a good social integration. unfortunately, the amendment was not approved by the committee, but i still strongly believe that it would be very useful. i also proposed that officials who, in the course of their work, frequently come into contact with citizens of other member states should be encouraged to learn a second european language. i think this is a good thing, given the migration of labour within europe, but also tourist mobility. only in this way can we encourage intercultural communication and understanding, the core values of the european union.
i would like to congratulate all the rapporteurs on the preparation of the regional development package. i would like to congratulate mr van nistelrooij in particular on his extraordinary efforts. it has very well captured in the motion for a resolution the need for member states to implement measures aimed at achieving territorial cohesion. the green paper also emphasises that, alongside social and economic cohesion, territorial cohesion policy is one of the main objectives of the european union. european regions develop differently if they are not coordinated through a single policy at union level. territorial cohesion is a key element in the process of european integration and achieving convergence between regions. i believe that both now and in the future, special attention must be paid to the convergence regions in the union so that, in the shortest possible time, the existing wide disparities are significantly reduced. in my country, romania, there has been significant progress in the development of the regions, but we are faced with disparities both between and within them, and between the rural and urban environment. sustainable and balanced development of the regions must take place in conditions of efficient use of the resources specific to each area. for example, the western part of romania is characterized by the existence of numerous geothermal springs. by allocating sufficient funds to the region for the production of alternative electricity and the use of geothermal water, new jobs will be created and numerous economic benefits will be obtained. i consider the package discussed today to be particularly important for romania as well.
i would like to welcome first the idea of a strengthened debate on cohesion. i congratulate each of our colleagues on their work and on the proposals they have made. i will make a few comments on some of the issues territorial cohesion first. the fundamental issue is to ensure the harmonious development of all the territories of the european union, the partnership between urban and rural areas, in order to stop losing territory and respond to the depopulation of rural areas. in the absence of a definition of territorial cohesion, which parliament is awaiting, the integrated concept of economic, social and territorial cohesion is the basis for the future regional policy of the union and the format of the structural funds after 2009. as regards the krehl report, i support all the proposals in the report which support the european regions and concern the removal of obstacles, the simplification of procedures and their stability over time, as well as the proposal to create concentrated methods of interregional exchange of good practice. as regards the urban dimension of cohesion policy, we know that there is no common definition of urban. we also know that there are about 5 000 cities in europe with fewer than 50 000 inhabitants. romania has a significant number of such human settlements. i believe that for these types of urban settlements we need a development model and adequate resources, because they are the ones that are missing or not benefiting from the effects of the polycentric approach. as part of territorial cohesion, integrated sustainable urban development will, under the new treaty, be managed jointly by the member states and the union. local and regional authorities must be prepared for this approach, which is already established as multi-level governance. i support the idea of a mandatory minimum level per inhabitant of the funds allocated of eur 1000 compared to 500 in the previous period.
in 2010, the commission and the member states will review the way the structural funds are used and their absorption rate. i call on the member states to carefully redefine the priorities they have and intend to use the structural funds for. i believe that urban mobility, rural development, energy efficiency of buildings and the development of transport infrastructure should be among the priorities of the member states for the use of the structural funds for the period 2011-2013. as rapporteur for the energy efficiency of buildings, i called for the share of the erdf that member states can use for social housing and for increasing the energy efficiency of buildings to be increased from 3 to 15%. this would mean greater flexibility for member states and the possibility of accelerating the absorption of european funds to improve the quality of life of european citizens. especially in this period of crisis, public funds, and in particular the structural funds, must be used by member states to ensure economic development and job growth.
the structural and cohesion funds are a subject of intense debate for us, an opportunity that is much praised but unfortunately under-exploited. the reasons are many, ranging from bureaucracy, cumbersome or short-lived rules, difficult access to information and lack of transparency. i can tell you that many of the romanian applicants complain about problems related to the eligibility of expenditure, rules that are valid for too little time, cumbersome documentation and, of course, long deadlines for project evaluation. i am glad that the european commission has also begun to recognise these obstacles and that the proposals for amending the regulations, especially in the context of the economic crisis, include provisions to simplify the rules for the use of these funds. this is a first step and i would like to think that many of our proposals will be taken up by the commission. the solution to these problems is twinning and technical assistance programmes, but as i have argued in my amendments to mrs krehl's report, a programme at union level is needed. in writing. micro-credit and even loans to entrepreneurs from community funds are an institutional lever that can and must compensate for the gap left by commercial banks as a result of the financial crisis that is already hitting the real economy. a commercial bank is only useful to the economy as long as it provides credit, which is not the case today, despite the massive infusion of public money into various banks. in these circumstances, i propose that member states should no longer directly finance (troubled) commercial banks, so that they can cover their huge losses and/or improve their financial ratios with public money, to the delight of their shareholders and as a basis for even generous bonuses; it is right that they should not be left to the brink of bankruptcy. my proposal is to use commercial banks as mere intermediaries, commissioners in the granting of loans and micro-loans from public money to economic agents, entrepreneurs who, without financing, are also subject to the risk of bankruptcy. in conclusion, loans and microcredit should reach those who need them through banks, but not through their balance sheets, but only by using their expertise and network to facilitate the contracting of such financing.
in writing. improving access to micro-credit for business development for small entrepreneurs, the unemployed and disadvantaged people who want to start their own business and who do not have access to traditional banking lending instruments, together with the recent decision to reduce vat on some services, are solutions that the european union is putting at the disposal of member states to overcome the crisis. the latest analysis suggests that the services, agriculture and tourism sectors may represent the areas that can absorb a significant part of the available labour force on the labour market, including unemployed people, which is why romania and the other eu countries need to develop the necessary tools to apply this idea, especially within the non-banking market segment. i believe that these microcredits can be successfully used to develop services for businesses, individuals or households from computer scientists to window washers, gardeners, elderly and childcare workers and can help to bring skills and personal qualities to life in a successful business. a micro-credit can be accessed by companies with less than 10 employees. it's good for people who want to work and unemployed people who want to start a business. micro-enterprises account for 91% of european companies.
in writing. the green paper on territorial cohesion, entitled 'transforming territorial diversity into an asset', launches a broad consultation with regional and local authorities, associations, ngos and civil society in order to promote a common understanding of this new concept and its implications for the future regional policy of the eu, but does not provide a definition of 'territorial cohesion'. territorial cohesion aims to ensure the harmonious development of all eu territories and to enable all citizens to make the most of the inherent characteristics of these territories. the green paper proposes that diversity be turned into a tangible asset and competitive advantage, contributing to the sustainable development of the whole eu, and makes special reference to the need for effective governance of cohesion policy in order to make it more flexible. the main challenge is to help the territories to harness their capital and to exchange good practice. the report by mr van nistelrooij covers this vast area of territorial cohesion and provides useful consideration of the commission's communications in this area. the green paper on territorial cohesion thus remains open to new challenges, but it is transformed into an effective instrument for partnerships and the exchange of good practice.
in writing. cohesion policy and rural development measures are subsumed by the same principle of solidarity promoted by the european project and contribute to the achievement of the objectives of the lisbon strategy. our analyses and decisions must take account of the different levels of agricultural development in the european union and the share of this sector in the economies of the member states, as well as the different situation of regional cohesion and development. i welcome the fact that the final version of this report includes my proposal to allow greater flexibility in the use of the structural funds so that they complement rural development measures. to ensure coordination and complementarity between cohesion policy and rural development measures, member states are required to put in place mechanisms to encourage the consistent and equitable use of european funds. at the same time, the european commission, through the instruments at its disposal, must better monitor the use of european funds at regional level, so as to ensure that rural areas are not harmed. this report is a first analysis of this issue, but it needs to be continued in order for the next financial perspective to ensure better coordination between eu financial support measures.

in writing. − the present commission proposal to amend directive 98/8/ec on the placing of biocidal products on the market has become necessary after an evaluation of its implementation showed that the 10-year period until 14 may 2010 for evaluating active substances used in biocidal products for inclusion in the community positive list will not be sufficient. consequently, the transitional period during which the market for biodegradable products will continue to be regulated by national rules would expire without the establishment of the community positive list. in practice, this would mean that important products such as disinfectants used in hospitals should be withdrawn from the market as from 15 may 2010. i voted in favour of this report because the extension of the current transition period allows the evaluation of active substances used in biodegradable products to be completed and provides an adequate period of time for member states to transpose the provisions and to issue authorisations and registrations for these products, and for the industry to prepare and submit complete dossiers. this extension also allows the principle of waste prevention (non-evaluated substances become waste) to be applied and the illegal marketing of biodegradable products to be avoided.

the reporter. − the single european sky ii package addresses the entire air transport system, with direct and positive implications for airlines, air navigation service providers, traffic controllers, airports, the aviation industry. it is the legislator's response to the need to harmonise and make european airspace and air traffic more efficient for the benefit of the environment, industry and, above all, passengers. the agreement reached with the council on the ses ii package is a step forward in the process of strengthening the european union. it is a natural step after the common market, after the adoption of the single currency, after the creation of the schengen area. we will have an air schengen from 2012. routes will be shorter, traffic control more efficient, air navigation services optimised and, in the future, integrated. as a result, flights will be shorter, fuel consumption will be lower, carbon dioxide emissions will be lower, which should normally lead to lower airfare. the compromise reached in the negotiations with the council reflects the need to accelerate the establishment of functional aerospace blocks. we have reached an agreement on the deadline for the fab to become operational, which is six months ahead of the european commission's original proposal. the fab operation is the main element in creating the single european sky, which is why i welcome the agreement concluded last november for the most important fab, the one for central europe. i hereby request the support of the european commission for the approval of the project related to the danube romania - bulgaria fab within the ten-t financial framework. with the support of the representatives of the french and czech presidencies, whom i thank, we have succeeded in balancing the decision-making and powers between the member states and the european commission, particularly with regard to the performance scheme, a key element of the ses ii package. the commission will decide on the harmonisation and the correct implementation of the targets contained in the national performance plans. the commission's initial proposal was supplemented by two elements introduced by parliament. the first of these is the coordinator of the functional aerospace block system. i considered it necessary, following the ten-t model, to appoint a coordinator to facilitate the conclusion of fab operating agreements, thus speeding up the process of unifying european skies. the second element concerns the clarification of the concept of 'joint projects' and the definition of their funding sources. the european parliament has also succeeded in imposing a strong emphasis on the human factor. the compromise reached with the council further clarifies the interdependencies between ses ii and the easa, given that the extension of the agency's responsibilities to airports, atm/ans and atc is in fact the 'security' component of the package. i consider it very important that a clear and complete definition has been found for the aerodromes covered by the provisions of this regulation. the new specifications issued by easa should be similar to the existing ones. in addition, the possibility was given to maintain the derogations granted so far. we also obtained the introduction of provisions on the need to strengthen and extend the consultation process with all stakeholders. the reports to be voted on tomorrow represent an important step forward in creating the single european sky and i am convinced that they are a success and a win-win for all concerned.

vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. i am pleased to inform the members of the european parliament that there is indeed progress in the harmonization of mobile phone chargers in europe. but first i would like to thank mr cappato and mr manders for their great commitment to tackling this problem, which is a daily reality for the citizens of europe. i agree with them completely that the much-complained inflation of chargers must end and that mobile phones must be powered by a single, standardised charger. hundreds of millions of useless chargers and adapters in europe are a senseless environmental burden and a costly nuisance to consumers. if you change your phone today, you usually need a completely different charger. even different models from the same manufacturer often cannot be charged with a single adapter. the subject is not new. however, it is important to note that charging a mobile phone is not a simple refuelling operation but a technically complex one. a few years ago, the technology was not yet mature enough to allow full harmonisation. charging a cell phone could cause it to overheat or even explode. these difficulties have now been overcome. so there are no longer any technical reasons against harmonization. i have therefore taken concrete steps to encourage industry to bring a single charger to the market. i am confident that the industry will move quickly now but we as european institutions must stay on top of the ball and we must not rule out possible legal regulation under any circumstances. as you may know, the network operators announced at their last congress in barcelona that they expect that by 2012, most of the new mobile phones they will be selling will be powered by a single, standardized charger. that's good, but it's not enough! the commission wants full harmonisation on the basis of a single standard and a binding commitment from industry to do so. the commission expects the industry to reach a binding agreement in the form of a memorandum by the end of april. this memorandum is to be signed by the major mobile phone manufacturers and ensure that every charger is capable of charging every mobile phone and every mobile phone can be charged by every charger. the commission will not hesitate to make a legislative proposal if industry does not reach a voluntary agreement. i expect that for other devices, like digital cameras or mp3 players, the problem will resolve itself automatically once the breakthrough for mobile phones is achieved. if that is not the case, then legal action is also needed. the commission is continuing to count on the valuable support of the european parliament so that we can finally put an end to this nuisance.
on behalf of the pse group. indeed, the issue we are discussing will affect a very large number of consumers across the european union. i have to appreciate that 2009 is the year of creativity and innovation, and that if this voluntary agreement between the mobile phone manufacturers is signed, a step towards standardisation can be made. i think that first of all we need to have a common technical standard, i think it is important that the european institutes dealing with standardization should also be involved, so that research can really be applied at market level. i also think it's important to have a consumer awareness campaign, because it's not enough just to have this energy-efficiency labeling on mobile phones, but i think it's important to have a consumer awareness campaign on the type of charger for mobile phones. 2012 is not far away. i think if manufacturers really invest in this new type of single charger, there's enough time to meet the 2012 deadline. however, i would like to mention that research has already led to the emergence of some applications on the market, namely chargers that allow two or three terminals to be charged in proximity. even if they are terminals of different types, of different brands, it is possible to charge them simultaneously. so we have to invest more in research, i think especially in research in the communications and information technology sectors. progress is being made; in the seventh framework programme for research we have a lot of money, but in a very narrow field, namely mobile phone chargers, not enough has been done, and that is why this protocol between manufacturers is a step forward, but it must be accompanied by common standards.
i would first like to congratulate the rapporteur on her work in establishing the legal framework for the implementation of the biometric identification system. some aspects of this report have sparked heated debate in many eu member states, particularly those relating to biometric identification. such disputes have recently occurred in romania, which is the penultimate country in the european union to introduce biometric passports, but the first to implement a new biometric standard with fingerprints on both hands and facial expression. the concern for the adoption of biometric identification is based on the natural concern for ensuring the security of individuals, as well as the concern for how the data obtained are used and protected. one of the most important duties of the member states is to ensure the safety of their citizens without endangering fundamental human rights. so i think it's our duty to find a way to balance the two essential elements of our lives: freedom and security. the report we are debating today is a rather technical one, designed to harmonise measures at european level on biometric identification. this is necessary as a number of member states already practice this method in the absence of a european legislative framework in this field. the fact that, for example, children under 12 and persons who are physically unable to be fingerprinted will be exempted from fingerprinting for biometric visas is a sign of moderation and pragmatism that needs to be extended to all member states.
council decision no 512 of 8 june 2004 established the legal framework for the capture of biometric data for the identification of persons. the european regulation under discussion defines common standards for the collection of biometric data for the identification of persons and is based on the relevant provisions of the international civil aviation organisation. the united kingdom and ireland will not apply the provisions of this regulation as the schengen acquis does not apply to them. i think it is important for this regulation, in particular, to respect the protection of personal data. in practice, the storage and processing of this data must be done in compliance with specific european legislation and also the fact that member states are responsible for organising the reception and processing of visa applications gives member states a very high responsibility to respect the rights of individuals. i just want to mention that it is extremely important that the processing and collection of this data is done by authorized personnel and under no circumstances is it used for other purposes.
member of the commission. − madam president, i would just like to thank, once again, baroness ludford and all the honourable members for their contributions and their comments. i shall convey to my colleague mr barrot all that they have said today.
in writing. the introduction of biometric identification data in the vis is an important step in establishing a secure link between the visa holder and the passport, thus preventing the phenomenon of using a false identity. however, this regulation has since its first reading pointed to a number of disagreements between the council and parliament on issues such as: fingerprinting of children up to the age of 6 years with the risk of ignoring details on the costs and inconveniences that parents would face once the children's fingerprints were changed; the new challenges in organising the collection of biometric data and, last but not least, the lack of experience of the member states in managing the retention of personal data and technical errors. in this context, we need to ensure that the member states apply uniform rules for issuing schengen visas and the common consular instructions are adapted and redefined. furthermore, particular attention needs to be paid to the protection of biometric data of those who have provided it. we must be aware that although this biometric data collection system is intended to combat crime and terrorism by providing access and exchange of information between police authorities of the member states, it could be equally accessible to different interest groups if high security measures are not provided for and taken.
in writing. the regulation amending the common consular instructions on visas defines the legal framework necessary for the introduction of biometric identifiers into the visa information system (vis) and the organisation of the reception and processing of visa applications. the regulation creates the possibility of cooperation with an external service provider for the purpose of collecting visa applications. i consider that the reasons for the free hand of cooperation with external providers are unfounded and create the danger of visa trafficking. although the regulation states that member states remain the 'controller' and external service providers the 'proxy holder', i believe that the protection of individuals with regard to the processing and movement of biometric data is called into question. the right to charge a service fee, in addition to the normal visa fee, will create differences between member states in the cost of a visa. i am absolutely convinced that this will create differences between member states and in the number of visa applications. i call on member states that practice 'outsourcing' as a form of organisation of the reception and processing of visa applications to take this risk into account and to review their legal framework in order to minimise the possibility of visa applications being collected by external providers.
member of the commission. − madam president, on 15 january 2008, the commission submitted its proposal on novel foods to the council and the european parliament, with the aim of simplifying the administrative burden for food-business operators when requesting pre-market approval for innovative food products. the current proposal maintains the principle of the need for pre-market authorisation for innovative products, to reassure consumers that new breeding or new production techniques are safe for humans and animals and respect the environment and consumers’ interests. the proposal streamlines and speeds up the authorisation process through a centralised food safety evaluation by efsa and sets precise deadlines at every stage of the procedure. it also includes an improved safety assessment, tailor-made to different types of foods, thereby allowing safe traditional food from third countries to enter the eu more easily. i would like to welcome the work of parliament, whose report addresses major issues concerning the development of a safe food sector. i would particularly like to confirm my support for the following principles: the need for a definition of engineered nanomaterials and the clarification that all such products require a case-by-case authorisation by the eu institutions; and the confirmation of the fact that food products from cloned animals are novel foods and therefore cannot be placed on the market without having been assessed by efsa and authorised through a regulatory procedure. i look forward to hearing your opinions on these sensitive issues and would like to thank the rapporteur, ms liotard, and the shadow rapporteurs for their valuable work on this important report.
on behalf of the alde group. – madam president, novel food regulations should provide for the diversification of food products on the european market, while ensuring that these new products are safe for the consumer. however, under the current regulation very few novel foods are approved on the eu market due to highly complex application and assessment procedures. if we had applied the current procedures to the authorisation of the potato or the kiwi fruit we might not have them on our table today. the revision of the current regulation should aim to set up a more efficient and practicable system for the authorisation of novel foods. i understand some of my colleagues’ concerns about allowing on the market new products that might present a danger or mislead the consumer. however, we should not fall into the trap of safety hysteria and kill innovation, and we should not discriminate against novel food, placing it a less favourable position than products already on the market that do not necessarily have a nutritional advantage for consumers; nevertheless, consumers have freedom of choice. my group is generally satisfied with the outcome of the vote in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety. however, there are certain issues that go far beyond the scope of this regulation, and consequently we will not be able to support it. for example, we cannot demand that a novel food has no negative impact on the environment. whether we like it or not, all human activities have an impact on the environment, and such a provision is disproportionate in this context. instead, my group believes we need to strike the right balance between encouraging innovation and applying the precautionary principle concerning food safety, consumer and environmental protection and animal welfare. our approach was to ease the long and bureaucratic procedures for putting novel foods on the market and protecting the industry’s investments by means of the interests of consumers by reinforcing implementing measures on, for example, marketing and monitoring, supporting the exclusion of cloned animals from the food chain, and specific labelling provisions. on the issue of cloning, i strongly support the exclusion of foods from cloned animals and their descendants from the scope of this regulation, and call on the commission to ban cloned animals in the food chain. in september 2008 the european parliament adopted by a large majority a resolution asking for a ban on cloned animals from the food supply. we must be consistent in the in writing. in my view, the health of both the present and future generations should be of concern to all of us. clean surroundings and atmosphere promote health. all scientific studies point to the fact that the ozone layer is extremely important, not only for the health of the population, but also for the maintenance of life on earth. unfortunately, there are a number of substances emitted into the atmosphere that destroy the ozone layer, contributing to the greenhouse effect. although there is evidence of a recovery in the ozone layer as a result of the measures taken, it is not expected that the pre-1980 level of ozone in the atmosphere will be reached until after the middle of the 21st century. i therefore fully support further measures to limit or even ban ozone-depleting substances. i believe that by doing so we are doing our duty not only to this generation but to future generations.
