the reporter. − the community computer system eurodac became operational in january 2003 and is designed to compare the fingerprints of asylum seekers and certain third country nationals or stateless persons. this system ensures the correct, accurate and timely application of the dublin regulation, which aims to establish an efficient and operational mechanism for determining responsibility for asylum applications lodged in one of the member states of the european union. eurodac is a computerised database containing the fingerprints of applicants for international protection aged 14 or over. this report aims to improve the efficiency of the system and to address the problems identified in the evaluation of the first years of operation. we have developed a number of effective and practical solutions to the problems of the collection and transmission of dactyloscopic data by member states. in the first stage, fingerprints are collected within 48 hours of the asylum application being lodged, and in the second stage, member states send the data thus obtained to the eurodac central system within 24 hours. the report shall include provisions allowing for the extension of the 48-hour period in exceptional cases, such as: where a quarantine period is required due to a serious contagious disease, where fingerprints have been destroyed, and in cases of well-founded and proven force majeure, for as long as these circumstances persist. the report advocates the establishment as soon as possible of a decentralised management agency for eurodac, the vis and sis ii, to ensure the most efficient operation of these systems. the management agency shall develop a common set of requirements to be met by persons authorised to access eurodac infrastructure and information. provisions were also introduced to prohibit the provision of data recorded in eurodac to the authorities of any other unauthorised third country, in particular to the country of origin of the applicants for protection, in order to protect the family members of asylum seekers from the serious consequences to which they might be exposed. in drafting the report, we aimed to establish rules to ensure that the system operates as efficiently and as quickly as possible, while at the same time protecting personal data and fundamental human rights. last but not least, i would like to thank my shadow rapporteurs, with whom i have worked very well, and my colleagues in the libe committee, who voted for the report by a large majority. a thank you to the amendment authors. i would like to note the excellent cooperation with the council and the european commission, to whom i am grateful.
the reporter. - i come from a country, romania, which until 1989 was ruled by a totalitarian and, i might say, murderous communist regime. this regime has kept its citizens in a big prison. yet, tens of thousands of people risked their lives to flee and seek political asylum. i know a lot of these destinations, and i know how important international protection is, the protection of the institution of political asylum. but it is essential that we identify the real asylum seekers, the ones who really have a legitimate claim for political asylum. and, by improving the recording system, obviously we can solve these cases much faster. but i would also like to discuss another problem in parallel, namely that of networks, the criminal criminality of networks of asylum-seekers. there are networks that make huge amounts of money transporting asylum seekers to the member countries of the european union. and i think that the fight against this criminal phenomenon should be a priority concern and a strategy should be developed to combat this phenomenon.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i would not like to leave without an answer - even though i have no really satisfactory answer to give - to mr busuttil, or to the italian members who have spoken, mr borghezio, mr catania and all the others; i would like to say, however, that the problem in the mediterranean is not a problem that can be confined to malta and italy. it is really necessary for europeans to realize the increasingly tragic and dramatic situation that has been exposed here. i myself went to lampedusa and malta. i met the two ministers in brussels on the occasion of an initial incident. we have, thank god, managed to find a solution. but i will raise the matter again with all the interior ministers at the jha council in early june. we will try to help malta and italy as much as we can, but it is true that there must be a european awareness, a european awareness of all the member states, of a situation which cannot be left to the sole responsibility of two member states. and so we have to think; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
in writing. eurodac is a key tool for managing information on applicants for international protection and immigrants who have either been detained for illegally crossing the border or are overstaying their legal stay in a member state. the reform of the eurodac regulation will address difficulties related to the effectiveness of its legislative provisions, such as the late transmission of fingerprints to the eurodac central system by certain member states, the exchange of data on refugees recognised in a given member state and the vague designation of the authorities having access to the eurodac database. i believe that a more efficient use of the eurodac database will only be possible when eurodac uses the same technical platform as sis ii and vis. the biometric matching system should be common to sis ii, vis and eurodac in order to ensure their interoperability and cost efficiency. i ask the commission to submit the necessary legislative proposals to establish an agency responsible for managing the three it systems, so that these tools can be brought together in a single location and that optimal synergy between them can be ensured in the long term, thus avoiding overlap and lack of coherence.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i thank the three rapporteurs and i would first like to turn to mr zwiefka and mr deprez. the commission is of course pleased that compromises have been found. however, it is true that there have been intensive negotiations since february and that agreement has been reached at first reading on the two proposals presented by the commission at the end of 2008. this is a very sensitive area for all the institutions involved - commission, council, european parliament - as mr deprez has very well emphasised. i thank all the parties for having reached a text which seems to us to respect the institutional prerogatives of the commission and, at the same time, to be a response to the legitimate expectations of the member states and parliament. but i would like to remind you that this is an exceptional procedure, limited in scope and time, and that the exclusive competence of the community in the matters concerned must, in any event, continue to be respected. i am very firm on this point and i agree with what mr deprez said, that the member states should not use this opportunity to take back certain powers and to encourage the commission to give up proposing in a certain way. i think we can agree on that. however, it is also true that this flexibility will enable the member states, in the absence of the exercise of community competence, to benefit from an institutional framework to facilitate citizens' access to justice in third countries, especially in the field of family law. yes, we must think - mr zwiefka and mr deprez alluded to this - of the rules on divorce, child custody, visitation rights, maintenance obligations and the difficult situations which can arise in the absence of legislation which is universally applicable to these matters at international level. the proposal on the law applicable to contractual and non-contractual obligations could also have a positive effect on solving very concrete, very specific problems, such as those connected, for example, with road and river traffic, as well as with the management of airports situated on the borders of several states, such as the basle-mulhouse-fribourg airport. however, this is another application of this institutional framework, which must, once again, remain exceptional. i would like to thank the rapporteurs of the juri and libe committees for their work and for their understanding, which has enabled this agreement to be reached before the end of the mandate of this parliament. i now turn to the pagano report, whose approach and content i share. i welcome the growing involvement of parliament in the field of criminal justice, not only in legislative action but also in designing the future of the european area of criminal justice. thank you, mrs pagano, for supporting our work at the moment, as we prepare the stockholm programme and will be publishing a communication containing recommendations for the period 2010-14. and i am glad that your report fully supports the principle of mutual recognition. it is thanks to the principle of mutual recognition that the union has achieved important successes, the european arrest warrant, and all this outlines a real area of criminal justice. the report also mentions the problems encountered in implementing the principle of mutual recognition and it is true that it is necessary to ensure the coherent and complete transposition and application of the many existing instruments which are based on the principle of mutual recognition. but it is true that there can be no mutual recognition without strengthening mutual trust between the judicial authorities of the member states. it's really the first ingredient of mutual recognition. i therefore thank the european parliament for advocating the creation of a genuine common judicial culture, as you have just said, mrs pagano. you have rightly stressed the development of training for the judicial professions, training in european mechanisms, relations with the court of justice, the use of mutual recognition instruments, judicial cooperation and comparative law. i fully agree with your report on this point, because i believe that in the stockholm programme the training of judges and the exchange of judges between member states will be the key to the future of this european area of law which we so dearly wish to see. of course, we will also use the justice forum, which is a meeting place for the various networks of legal professionals, which plays a key role in making practitioners aware of the european dimension of their work and, with the help of the union, well, these practitioners must cooperate to really exchange best practice. the commission also agrees with the proposal put forward in the report really, thank you for an evaluation mechanism which is not limited to the transposition of union instruments but which covers the state of justice in the member states more generally. how effective, how rapid, how much respect for the defence guarantees? work on this subject has already begun with the idea, launched by the dutch minister of justice, to create an evaluation mechanism on the state of the functioning of justice, on compliance with the principles of the rule of law, while, of course, using existing material and providing added value in terms of political monitoring. these assessments would allow recommendations to be made. the commission also supports greater involvement of the european parliament in its evaluation mechanisms. mr deprez, this would be an opportunity to involve parliament in the work of the groups of experts which we will be setting up this year and in the years to come. and then you mention the transposition of the new eurojust decision. here again we agree with the approach suggested in the report, with the usefulness of an implementation plan and of expert meetings with the member states. this is what will ensure that the new eurojust decision is implemented swiftly. finally, the report stresses the need to make good use of new technologies. the european e-justice strategy was launched to exploit the potential of information and communication technologies in the field of justice. i can only thank the european parliament for its work and for the reflections it has given us in this area. i am also convinced that together we will succeed in building this area of criminal justice, this area of law which normally must be the result of a community of citizens who are rightly entitled to quality justice, regardless of the member state in which they are located.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i welcome this opportunity to speak on these three important legislative proposals, and am grateful to the rapporteurs for the extensive work which has gone into their reports. i would like first to comment on the first two proposals, and then to turn to the third proposal on the issue of the further development of criminal justice within the eu. the objective of the two proposals covered by the reports from mr zwiefka and mr deprez is to establish a procedure which will allow the member states to negotiate and conclude agreements with third countries on aspects of judicial cooperation in civil matters falling within the exclusive competence of the community. the first proposal, subject to the codecision procedure, covers applicable law in contractual and non-contractual obligations. the second, subject to the consultation procedure, covers certain matters in the area of family law. i would like to underline that the procedure put in place by the two future regulations is devised in such a way as to ensure the integrity of community law. before authorising the negotiation of an agreement, the commission will check that the envisaged agreement does not render community law ineffective or undermine the proper functioning of the system established by its rules. the commission will also check that the envisaged agreement does not undermine external relations policy as decided by the community. it could in fact be argued that, by making it possible for member states to negotiate and conclude agreements with third countries that are compatible with community law, the range of operation of community law is extended to countries outside the european union. the procedure established by the two proposals will apply primarily to the negotiation and conclusion of bilateral agreements between a member state and third countries. it will in certain cases, however, also apply to the negotiation and conclusion of regional agreements between more than one member state and/or more than one third country. as far as regional agreements are concerned, the procedure established by the proposal in the area of the family law will apply to the amendment or renegotiation of two already-existing conventions between the nordic states. in the proposal in the area of applicable law, only a few regional arrangements will in fact fall within its scope. these could cover, for example, the operation of an airport situated in a border area, waterways common to two or more countries, or cross-border bridges and tunnels. the procedure established in the two proposals is based on a high degree of trust and cooperation between the member states and the commission. a mechanism is provided to deal with those situations where the commission, on the basis of its assessment, reaches the conclusion that the negotiation or conclusion of an agreement should not be authorised. in such situations, the member state concerned and the commission will enter into discussions with the aim of finding a solution together. the presidency, on behalf of the council, hopes and expects that it will be possible to reach a first reading agreement on the proposal in the area of applicable law. constructive negotiations have taken place between the european parliament, the commission and the council, during which the three institutions have together managed to solve a number of difficult issues. as the proposal in the area of applicable law is largely identical to the proposal in the area of family law, it goes without saying that the amendments made to the first proposal have been taken over in the second proposal, even though that proposal is not subject to the codecision procedure. it is, in the interest of good law-making, highly desirable to maintain parallelism between the two texts. i would like to conclude with a few comments on parliament’s recommendation on the development of eu criminal justice, which is the subject of the report by ms pagano. the council very much agrees on the importance of mutual recognition as a cornerstone of judicial cooperation within the eu. we consider that it should both be broadened – by adopting other legal instruments in the future – and deepened, through a more effective implementation of the mutual recognition instruments adopted so far. in this context, the council would like to draw parliament’s attention to the fact that it is in the process of finalising the fourth round of mutual evaluations on the practical implementation of the european arrest warrant and the surrender procedures between the member states. within the context of this series of mutual evaluations, experts have also been studying the issues related to interaction between, on the one hand, the european arrest warrant, and, more generally, the principle of mutual recognition, and, on the other hand, the proportionality principle. however, the proportionality principle also has to be balanced with another principle, which is equally dear to parliament – namely that of subsidiarity. the reality is that judicial authorities in various member states have differing views on what constitutes a serious offence. the council looks forward to further work with parliament and the commission on the establishment of a system of horizontal and continuous evaluation and implementation of eu policies and legal instruments. on the issue of judicial training, the council shares parliament’s opinion that there is a need to foster a genuine eu judicial culture by, inter alia, promoting direct exchanges between judges, prosecutors and members of the judicial staff of different member states, and to actively develop the european judicial training network. the council also shares parliament’s view on the need for a swift and effective implementation of the new eurojust and europol decisions. by way of conclusion, i would like to thank parliament for the extensive and detailed work which has gone into the three reports before us this afternoon.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. after world war ii, national borders separated communities and families. i'm referring to a european example that's close to home. one part of szelmenc, formerly belonging to hungary, is now part of the territory of a european union member state, slovakia, under the name of nagyszelmenc, and the other part, kisselmenc, is in ukraine. until 23 december 2005, there was no border crossing between the two villages. for 60 years, parents, children, relatives lived apart without seeing each other for decades. the union has given them the opportunity they have been waiting for, the opening of the border crossing. the example cited is just one of many hundreds or thousands, and it is a powerful argument for why we are discussing this report now. the draft regulation establishes a procedure for jurisdiction between member states and third countries in matrimonial matters, matters of parental responsibility and matters relating to maintenance obligations. this regulation will not override community law, as it will apply only where the member state concerned demonstrates that it has a specific interest, in particular in relation to economic, geographical, cultural or historical links between the member state and the third country in question, in concluding the bilateral sectoral agreement with the third country. however, the commission notes that the proposed agreement has only a limited impact on the uniform and consistent application of the existing community rules and on the proper functioning of the system established by those rules. i would like to thank my colleague, mr deprez, for taking up this important subject which affects the lives of citizens of the union and those living outside the union, all the more so because the document strikes a balance between the legal powers of the community institutions and those of the national states.
mr president, tonight the hope generated by the czech ratification of the lisbon treaty is being overshadowed by the quasi-conspiratorial atmosphere of this meeting. some were afraid that by preparing the proper implementation of a treaty badly and urgently needed we might offend certain citizens of the union. i believe that, on the contrary, we are offending the citizens by hiding the truth about what europe really is, and could be, and by refusing a frank and rational dialogue with them. likewise, to show respect for a minority opinion while ignoring the majority decision is offensive to both the given majority and the general principles of democracy we all claim to cherish. the written text of a treaty is not enough. one has to give that text a clarifying interpretation which puts in light its spirit, thus allowing for the best implementation. that is precisely what today’s reports are doing. they speak about: one, the parliamentarisation of the union; two, the communitarisation of the european institutions; three, the establishment of an interinstitutional equilibrium as a guarantee for a transnational checks-and-balances system; four, the assurance of legislative coherence and cohesion at european union level through europeanisation of the national parliaments and not nationalisation of the european parliament; five, concentrations of instruments and policies for the good of institutional efficiency; and, six, the improvement of representation, transparency and participation at european union level. along those lines, we will be able to see emerging a demos which will fill with substance the present shell of the european procedures, making them relevant to the citizens. the only thing which remains to be done is to find a solution to bridge the elections to the new parliament and the coming into force of the lisbon treaty. i hope that the sense of responsibility and solidarity of our irish fellows will help us to achieve that, and to keep to our historical timetable.
in writing. there is only one small step left to take before the treaty of lisbon is adopted, which, once in force, will bring the european union much closer to its 500 million inhabitants. romania, the country i represent in the european parliament, is one of the first countries to ratify the treaty because its entire political class believes in the european construction. the european parliament elections will not be held under the auspices of the lisbon treaty, but this in itself demonstrates how democratic and representative the institution of the european community is and how important each of its nations is. european institutions, including the european parliament, are far too abstract for the citizen of the community at the moment. the importance of parliament in the union's decision-making process has increased with each european treaty. the lisbon treaty is no exception and creates a parliament with a significantly greater involvement in the legislative process. the treaty will bring the union closer to its citizens. each of us knows how difficult it is to bring the problems of the community to the attention of the citizens of our countries of origin. the fact that the european parliamentarians, who are directly elected by each member state, are given increased powers is, at the moment, the best solution for humanizing an institutional structure that is unique in the world.

the allocation of slots is a problem directly linked to the lack of airport capacity, especially at large airports. the economic crisis and the relative decrease in traffic caused by it only postpone, in the short term, the real problem, namely the difficulties created by the congestion of the large airport hubs and the potential congestion of small airports. we have a duty to find solutions to the problems of the moment, but we must not lose sight of solving the problems of the future. parliament called on the european commission to draw up a coherent master plan for airport capacity building. a number of european airports have such plans, but their coordination at european level, in the context of the newly approved single sky, is imperative. i am convinced that, with the creation of the european observatory last november, this will be achieved in the near future. this plan is essential for the sustainable development of the air transport sector, a vital sector for the european economy. the problem of slot machines is not just a european problem. the traffic at european airports does not come exclusively from europe. for this reason, the slot issue must also be resolved at international level, with the support of iata, eurocontrol and all stakeholders in this field. i therefore believe that the recommendation made today by parliament to the commission to re-examine in the near future the impact of the crisis on air traffic and to revise directive 95/93 in this context is the most appropriate formula we can propose at this uncertain time. without careful analysis, we risk unwarranted harm to both the principle of competition, which is fundamental to the economy, and to the emerging airlines, whose development still depends, unfortunately, on the 'use it or lose it' rule. the losers would be the passengers first, and that doesn't have to happen.

member of the commission. − this is a very timely question and i could answer very briefly that the priorities are agreement in copenhagen for reduction commitments by developed countries, nationally appropriate mitigation actions by developing countries, and finance. i would, however, like to say a few more words. we now have less than three months until copenhagen and the climate talks have now entered into a crucial phase. with 250 pages of negotiating text on the table, the negotiations have not yet gathered sufficient momentum to come to an agreement that is ambitious and detailed enough. however, among most parties there is a sense of urgency and the willingness to focus on areas of convergence. the ultimate objective of the climate agreement is to keep global warming below 2 degrees celsius, an objective that was endorsed at the last g8 summit and the major economies forum. we need comparable and more ambitious emission reduction targets for the group of developed countries, which in aggregate today offer less than 15% reduction as compared with 1990. this falls short of the 25-40% reduction required by science. we welcome the fact that japan will strengthen its target. the eu has offered to take up a 30% reduction target if others make comparable commitments. developing countries should take appropriate mitigation actions to curb the growth of their emissions to 15-30% below business as usual by 2020. the eu proposes that developing countries (except least developed countries) design and implement low carbon growth plans containing their key mitigation actions. these plans would then form the basis for targeted financial and other support. adequate international financing will be essential to reach an effective agreement in copenhagen. money will make or break the deal. we need to mobilise private investment and promote the establishment of a robust international carbon market, but substantial public funding will also be required. in this respect, it is worth mentioning the global partnership on technology, which aims at doubling investment in low carbon technologies. furthermore, we have to strengthen support to the poorest and most vulnerable countries to adapt to the increasing adverse effects of climate change. last week, on 10 september 2009, the commission adopted a communication on stepping up international climate finance, which aims at speeding up the international negotiations. there is a daunting task ahead of us, with intense negotiations over the coming months – but failure is not an option.

previously. regarding brazil, china, india, mexico and other developing countries, of course we expect from them a reduction in the rate of growth of their emissions of the order of 15% to 30% below have already taken national measures which will lead to reductions in emissions, either by energy efficiency measures or investments in renewable sources of energy, but we need to intensify our cooperation with them – exchange of information, cooperation regarding technologies and transfer of technology – in order to achieve the reductions that we need. regarding cost reduction and, as you mentioned, energy efficiency, clearly all investments in energy efficiency are win-win-win situations. for example by reducing the consumption of imported oil, not only do you save money, and you do european union’s policies. we do support policies that will improve the sanitary quality and supply of water, especially in very poor countries. regarding food, we were very careful, for example, when we examined the biofuels directive, that there should be no competition between feedstocks for food and biofuel. we always take account of these important issues. regarding the impact assessment and the issues of competitiveness, these were discussed at length when we adopted the energy and climate package. many studies have been carried out not only by the commission but also by industry and by various sectors. the provisions that we have in our legislation will provide the assurances need to preserve the competitiveness of other european industries, especially small and medium-sized enterprises by, for example, granting free allowances, in many cases up to 100% of their emissions. so this is something that we are taking into account and of course the same applies when we go to 30%. additionally, if we go to 30%, it will mean that we shall have an ambitious agreement in copenhagen where all developed countries will undertake similar comparable reduction targets to the european union and developing countries will accept mitigation actions which will create a level playing field for the whole world. we shall then have comparable reduction obligations which will mean that the problem of competitiveness will not exist.

i support the european commission's decision, which gives substance to the commitment made for years to lift the visa requirement for people from the western balkans. however, i believe that the citizens of the republic of moldova should enjoy the same rights of free movement in the eu as soon as possible. the european union must continue to develop its open door policy towards these countries, and the abolition of visas is an important step towards the european integration of these peoples. in addition to this decision, which will lead to the development of cross-border business opportunities and the free movement of persons, the european institutions should consider cultural and educational programmes that make european values known in these countries. in this context, ensuring border security and combating international crime must remain a priority. finally, i would like to reiterate that romania has not recognized kosovo's independence.
madam president, the liberalisation of the visa regime for the western balkan countries is important, as this measure matters most to ordinary citizens in the region and it will clearly show the benefits of the eu rapprochement process. i am confident that the conditional inclusion on the white list of albania and bosnia and herzegovina will prove to be a strong incentive for meeting the rest of the benchmarks on the road map. in our case, back in 2001, such a strong signal was sent, and in a couple of months we managed to fulfil all pending conditions. it is essential that albania and bosnia and herzegovina are included on the schengen white list as soon as possible, and the commission should provide all the necessary technical assistance to the authorities of these two countries in order to meet the necessary conditions in a short while.
in writing. the european commission and the european council are called upon to take a decision soon on the opening of the european area to the citizens of macedonia, serbia and montenegro. the moment is very important for over ten million europeans who want a visa to cross the union border. macedonia was with europe when europe needed it. and serbia understood that europe wanted her to join, but for that she had to make peace with her recent past. serbia has cooperated closely with international institutions such as the international criminal court and has taken responsibility for its past mistakes. it is time for europe to reward the efforts of these countries to align themselves with the democratic and economic requirements that characterize the union of 27. their journey has not been easy, and their efforts must be appreciated for what they have done. macedonia, serbia and montenegro have definitely entered the european game and therefore i believe that the eu should decide in favour of lifting the visa requirements for the citizens of these three countries. their governments have demonstrated that they share the same values as us, and a favourable decision would give new impetus to much-needed internal reforms in macedonia, serbia and montenegro.
in writing. i welcome the commission's initiative to abolish the visa system for citizens of the western balkans region, namely the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, serbia and montenegro. such measures, which aim to bring these states closer to the eu with a view to integration, will significantly reduce the conflict-inducing potential of the area. for romania, which shares a border with serbia, such a move can only be an additional guarantee of friendly cross-border relations. it is a measure which will contribute to greater freedom of movement for the romanian population in romania and serbia and which will contribute to the development of trade relations between our country and serbia and montenegro. i am confident that the visa liberalisation for the three countries mentioned above is only the beginning of the process, with the measures later extended to albania and bosnia and herzegovina. although they do not meet the commission's requirements, i believe that through coordinated efforts the results will soon become visible. before concluding, i would like to stress that visa liberalisation and the free movement of people in the western balkans should not cause fear, but rather the conviction that the european security area is expanding to our benefit, to the benefit of all.
, in writing. the european union has grown stronger with each enlargement, not only by creating a common market for almost 500 million citizens, but also by ensuring stability in central and eastern europe. the balkan countries are an integral part of europe. the economic crisis or the ratification of the lisbon treaty should not delay these countries' accession to the eu. i am convinced that enlargement towards the balkans is a vital process which the union must sustain in order to strengthen its global role. it should not be forgotten that the integration of the balkan countries, together with the healing of the bloody wounds of the war at the end of the 20th century, ensures the stability of the european union and the prosperity of the region. the abolition of the visa requirement for serbia, montenegro and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia is a key step in the process of their accession, but also reflects the union's commitment to the region. the process must be pursued with purpose. this will allow bosnia and herzegovina, albania and, in due course, kosovo to benefit from the early application of the visa waiver, once the conditions are fulfilled. i unreservedly share the view of those european politicians who believe that the failure of the balkan countries to join would have unforeseeable, harmful consequences for the european union.
acting president of the council. - this is a very difficult question to answer. we will be at the g20 meeting next week to initiate the first such discussion on exit strategies. but it is clear that the situation is very different in the different member states, and therefore there will be slightly different timetables. i hope that we can start this process quite soon, but it also depends on the economic situation. we see light at the end of the tunnel, we think the worst is over, and then we need to move faster into this exit strategy thinking. if we do not do this eventually, it is the very most vulnerable in our societies who will suffer from rising unemployment, austerity and the risk of inflation. but exactly when that time will occur in the various countries is a little early to say today.

combat unemployment such as the european social fund and the european globalisation adjustment fund. it is important to communicate to citizens what the eu is doing, both from the point of view of unemployment. these two instruments are important financial tools to respond to the current economic downturn and to increase employment by introducing integrated flexicurity strategies and ensuring that skills are upgraded and better matched to existing needs. this was expressed by the council in december 2008 when it supported the rapid introduction of complementary measures to support employment by the european social fund. the council also called for improvements to the procedures of the european globalisation adjustment fund. therefore, a review of the original regulation was carried out to enable the fund to respond more effectively to support for workers made redundant, not only as a result of globalisation but also temporarily as a result of the financial and economic cases where assistance from this fund has been granted.
president-in-office of the council. − yes, we have indeed discussed this in the council several times. there is a quite unanimous view that, for the sake of the quality of the project, there should be an element of national financing as well. therefore, the proposal to eliminate that has no support from the council. however, we are aware of the situation and of the problems. we have asked the commission to present an alternative proposal. i brought that up with commissioner samecki, who is responsible for it, just two days ago. they are working on such a proposal and will present it as soon as possible.
i regret that there is no support in the council for 100% funding when it comes to the european social fund to reduce unemployment, especially in this period of crisis. i would like to mention that in this period of economic crisis, there is, especially in the steel and shipbuilding industries, an increase in unemployment or even technical unemployment - not just redundancies, but technical unemployment. i would like to ask you, in view of the need to invest and to ensure the economic competitiveness of the european union in the future: what measures do you envisage to make it easier to use the european social fund and the european globalisation adjustment fund to support these industries in economic difficulty?
many voices have called for a freeze on milk production since the beginning of the crisis. such a measure would not only be unsuitable but would be wrong, at least from the following points of view. the commission notes that the milk quota is not a fixed amount, but is fixed by the milk levy. the quotas went up, the production went down. i don't see where the connection is. the market itself is the explanation for the fall in prices. i think that imposing rigid quotas would cause prices to rise over time. the beneficiaries will again not be the producers but the processors and traders. if we want to limit production, we should encourage producers to eventually voluntarily give up animal husbandry through incentives, rather than through measures that could distort the market. what will happen in the event of a freeze in quotas when, for example, demand on the world market resumes? what could european producers do? because the milk production doesn't have a tap to turn on and off... (the president interrupted the speaker) i was saying, what could european manufacturers do in the event of a resumption of demand on the world market? because the dairy doesn't have a tap that we can turn on and off at will. if we cut back now, people would obviously stop raising cows, and it would be very difficult to restore the herd when we realize that what some people now imagine to be a good measure is actually a big mistake.
in writing. we are now experiencing the most serious crisis in the milk sector, generated by the global crisis and representing basically the gap between demand and supply. the fall in milk and milk products prices affects primarily low-income farms; therefore, i do not think that the quota system should be frozen in all member states, but that each member state should decide how to set its own quotas. the problem is that, compared to 1983-84, only one-fifth of the producers remain on the market and now we risk another series of farms closing. so we need to take urgent action to prevent that from happening. to stop the crisis in this sector we should provide for the following: the extension of advance storage measures for butter, milk powder and cheese, the acceleration of the creation of a dairy fund to meet the needs of small producers and young farmers and an agreement with supermarkets to establish a decent price for agricultural producers as well as a decent price at the point of sale.
mr president, everyone wants energy security, so why do we not have it? maybe it is because there are 27 interpretations of what energy security means. personally, i interpret it as meaning, among other things, diversifying the sources and moving away from our gas dependency on russia. we do not have to look too far for evidence of this, just at some of our member states which, being too far from russia to have a pipeline, do not have all the problems attendant on dependency. i think we should focus on lng, developing technologies, building lng terminals and bringing gas from all over the world. we should also contribute to establishing a global market for lng such as there is for oil and commodities. concerning the nabucco pipeline, i think the project should be quickly redesigned to take into consideration gas from various sources, and reconsider a shorter route which might lead from georgia, ukraine, under the black sea to romania. we just have to look at the map. the fact that member states have different interpretations of, or interests in, energy security is also proven by the fact that some countries involved in nabucco have also signed up for south stream, thereby lowering nabucco’s credibility and the chances for a common european energy policy. south stream definitely means increasing dependency on russian gas.
in 2008, the european union's trade deficit reached a record high of eur 242 billion, mainly due to the increase in the price of imported energy. the nabucco project will pass through turkey, bulgaria, romania, hungary and austria and will supply the union with 30 billion cubic metres of natural gas from the caspian sea annually. the €200 million allocated to the european economic recovery plan is insufficient. we ask that the union significantly supplement the funds allocated. desertec will use solar energy from north africa and will include a mediterranean plan to capture solar energy and build an electricity transmission network linking the european union to the middle east and north africa. the union needs to invest more in diversifying its energy supply sources. as rapporteur for the energy performance of buildings, i call on the union to provide innovative financial instruments to stimulate investment in the use of renewable energy and energy efficiency, in particular for buildings and transport.
nabucco will provide a significant part of the european union's gas demand. but more importantly, the political aspect: it will eliminate dependence on a single source. repeated crises have shown that the current situation, with russia as the only source and ukraine as the only transit country, does not ensure the security of europe's economy and its citizens. the development of new energy supply routes must be as important as the development of relations with russia. the delay in starting the nabucco project was unfortunately due to the individual interests of some member states. member states must understand that the benefits of this project will not only benefit the countries they cross, or the participating companies, but all european citizens whose welfare and security national governments must ensure. the mistakes that have delayed this project must not be repeated in securing the gas supply. there are countries in the region such as azerbaijan, turkmenistan, kazakhstan, iraq, iran, who want to participate with their reserves to supply the pipeline. the commission must repeat what it has done for the intergovernmental agreement, namely participate in the next negotiations and reach a positive result as soon as possible. if we do not do it, others will, and it will certainly not be in the interests of the european citizens.
member of the commission. − mr president, it would be difficult for me to answer all the questions raised, but i would like to emphasise a couple of points. first of all, the policies we follow in the energy sector seek to promote the wellbeing of our citizens and our industry. what we are looking for is a secure supply of well-priced and clean energy. this is our overarching goal. secondly, we never make any side deals when we are discussing energy agreements. there are no compromises either on enlargement or on human rights. we work from the point of view that interdependence in energy supply is the most important thing and is beneficial for all – for suppliers, transit countries and consumers. it takes time to convince our partners, but that is the only way to achieve stability. thirdly, even if it sometimes seems that we are slow, i think that basing ourselves on the industry proposals, and on support for industry, is crucial because that makes us strong. perhaps it does not make us a speedboat in the energy ocean, but it makes for stability. when we make a change, we have a much broader basis for it, so we are much safer. all the projects have been well checked for cost efficiency and future viability. so i believe that is the right support to give. the next area where we have a weakness, and which we are continuing to discuss, is external energy policy and coherence. it is true that there is a lot of controversy – or at least perceived controversy – and, as a commissioner, i would definitely be happy to see a more coherent external energy policy. the motion for a resolution addresses exactly this issue because, although there is no in-built conflict between member states, there is perceived conflict. all the activities pursued by the member states also benefit the european union. so we should follow this up and really try to build a system where we speak with one voice, not only verbally but also in terms of the points of view that we want to emphasise. for this reason the second strategic energy review is still very important. all the points that we put forward in the second energy review are still there. at the same time, from the commission’s point of view, we clearly see that we cannot afford to move from interdependence to dependence. that is why we particularly support diversification projects like nabucco and lng – not that they completely change our relationship of interdependence with other countries, but they give us additional safety margins. so that is what we are doing, but at the same time we definitely take note of what happens in the energy world. regarding the point on nuclear energy, we have moved away from this option. we have adopted a nuclear safety directive but it is very much a national and very sensitive point. i really believe that, from the union point of view, we should build upon the cooperation of nuclear safety regulators and try to establish a safer and more coherent system. but i doubt that we could go further than that. last but not least, i really believe that these issues and debates very much help to shape energy policy, but there is no single instrument that provides for it. there are many instruments, and we will come back to this debate in the future. thank you very much for this debate. i will be very happy also to answer questions in the itre committee, or in any other committees that would like to discuss energy issues in more detail.
in writing. i welcome the progress made with the signing of the ankara agreement on the launch of the nabucco project and the protocol on the agreement on the launch of the desertec project. the nabucco project must be given priority as it is a solution to the problem of gas supply, which has become more acute in recent years. i know that while nabucco is such an important project geopolitically, there must also be strong business reasons for the partners in the project to make it a reality as soon as possible. the economic crisis that has reduced the money for investment by the participating companies, as well as some uncertainties about the supply sources of the pipeline, are obstacles that need to be overcome. the 200 million euros we are providing for the project are welcome, but in addition we need to step up political and diplomatic efforts with turkey and the countries in the region that supply gas. i also want to call on member states to show solidarity in order to prevent gas crises similar to those of recent years. we cannot afford to wait for the entry into force of the lisbon treaty and the completion of nabucco while europeans risk running out of gas in the middle of winter because of the russian-ukrainian dispute.
in writing. as we are at the beginning of our mandate, i believe that one of the areas in which the european parliament must be actively involved is in ensuring energy security. in this context, i would like to stress the importance of the nabucco project, which will help to ensure the energy security of the european union, as it will ensure that european consumers have access to alternative sources in a safe way. the signing on 13 july 2009 of the nabucco project agreement between austria, bulgaria, romania, turkey and hungary, representing the political commitment of the project's partner states to continue efforts to bring the pipeline to fruition, sent a positive signal to investors and natural gas supplying states. the countries involved in this project, together with the european commission, must continue to focus their efforts on attracting investment and securing viable suppliers for nabucco.
in writing. in addition to being the world's top gas exporter, russia has recently become the world's largest oil exporter, overtaking saudi arabia. this situation places moscow in a position of considerable influence, based on control of resources. but energy is a commodity, to which the principles of the market economy must be applied. energy must not be used as a tool of political pressure. the energy crises faced by europe have demonstrated the importance of diversifying energy sources. they also demonstrated the added value that nabucco represents in this respect for the whole of the european union. romania has been and remains a strong supporter of the nabucco project. in july, romania signed the intergovernmental agreement on the nabucco project, along with turkey, bulgaria, hungary and austria. we consider the conclusion of this agreement a success and an important step forward. a pipeline the size and ambition of nabucco will face many challenges before it becomes a reality. the only way to overcome these challenges is to persevere.
in writing. – we try hard to encourage a coherent energy policy, but such a policy exists and is fully implemented. there is only one small problem: it is not ours. it is russia’s. now, we have the french edf company signing into south stream. before that, we had the russians taking over the hungarian company mol’s interest in nabucco. and before that we had the austrian gas terminal in baumgarten being taken over by the mysterious centrex company. we need a clear, european energy policy, and we need it now. this is possibly our last opportunity to rally behind nabucco. otherwise, if the council and the commission remain neutral, they should be prepared for very cold winters and very hot politics.
mr. president, i voted for this resolution and i'll explain why. the european union is dependent on energy imports, consumption is constantly increasing, but natural reserves are limited. energy security requires both diversification of sources and transport routes and very efficient interconnection between member states, as is currently being done through eu-funded projects on the gas pipelines between romania and its neighbours, hungary and bulgaria. so i thought, well, here we are, but what else do we have to do? i would make a comparison, perhaps a bold one, but a simple one, with electricity. today, electricity comes into our homes without us knowing where it comes from. through a diversified natural gas network and multiple transmission networks, we must achieve exactly the same goal: gas security in any situation and regardless of the situation. that's why i supported and support the nabucco project but, in parallel, the shift towards diversification of renewable energy sources.
in writing. − the european union is currently experiencing one of the most serious crises in the milk sector, due to the increase in production and the significant drop in global demand. in view of the dramatic situation of european milk producers, it is necessary to continue the public intervention period (i.e. buying-in and storage of skimmed milk powder and butter) until at least february next year or until 2011, if deemed necessary. i do not think we can afford to see european farms disappear, because after a year we will have to import milk and milk products from outside the community, and if we take into account that the sanitary standards will in no way be what we want, we have far too much to lose. the report is welcome in this context, but to really solve the problem in the milk sector we must take related measures, because this stock involves the allocation of important resources and it may be that at some point the stock is useless. we need to invest now in sustainable agriculture that can provide the food we need, even in times of financial crisis, to prevent a food crisis later.
in writing. − we are at the beginning of our mandate, when we are setting the priorities for the future policies of the european union. i know that we are tempted to focus on some things that we consider to be of the utmost importance and to neglect others. in this respect, i would like to stress that we can give up a lot, but we cannot give up food, which is why agriculture must remain a priority for the eu. i believe that the amount of de minimis aid granted to farmers should be increased beyond the limit of eur 15 000 set by the commission and that an increased budget should be allocated to promote the milk and milk products sector. i strongly recommend supporting milk and meat farmers to stabilise markets by including them in the temporary crisis framework for state aid. direct aid schemes also need to take account of the particularities of the new member states, where the agricultural sector plays an important role in the national economy, and to ensure that support for agriculture is maintained, so as to overcome structural problems and achieve the convergence objective by increasing the level of development in the agricultural sector, closing the efficiency and competitiveness gaps with the old member states.

in writing. the european union is moving rapidly towards the implementation of the most important reform in its history: the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. ireland said 'yes' to him, 16 months after the big 'no' that worried all the chancelleries of europe equally. the union now expects the polish president to ratify the treaty quickly, as he promised, and the czech constitutional court to do what the czech president refuses. the union will become a more flexible and responsive institution, but in addition the treaty offers a breathing space for aspiring member states. the western balkan states have strongly welcomed ireland's ratification of the treaty. the union's voice will become stronger internationally as its institutions are established and reformed. the union will no longer be just a common market but a power in international relations. the power is given by the 27 member states, which could become more in the not too distant future. the year 2010, when we hope the treaty will come into force, could be a year of rebirth for the union, which has known, throughout its history, to reinvent itself continuously.
in writing. the entry into force of the lisbon treaty will greatly simplify legislative procedures, the most important progress being the extension of the areas where decisions are taken by the eu council by qualified majority (instead of unanimity) and the extension of the areas where the european parliament has a co-legislatory role alongside the eu council. these innovations will greatly simplify decision-making at european level, especially in areas such as the structural funds and the cohesion fund, which are very important for romania, which needs this money to develop. in addition, it is a welcome fact that the european parliament will acquire greater powers, for example in the field of agricultural funds, an area so heavily affected by the economic crisis we are going through and, at the same time, an area where concrete and rapidly effective measures are needed to improve the lives of farmers and to ensure the food security of our citizens.
in writing. the lisbon treaty has put european issues on the agenda of national debates in national parliaments. in practice, each legislative proposal from the european commission will be examined by national parliaments to validate compliance with the principle of subsidiarity. if one third of the national parliaments refer the infringement to the commission, the commission is obliged to review its proposal. if one half of the national parliaments consider that their subsidiarity is being infringed, the european parliament and the council are obliged to decide whether this principle is being respected or not. after adoption of a european legislative act, national parliaments may, within two months of its publication, apply to the european court of justice for its annulment. given the length of the legislative process at european level, the inclusion of european issues on the agenda of national debates allows member states to receive signals and development directions in time and to be able to build at the same time as the eu. the lisbon treaty reaffirms that the eu economy is a social market economy and gives the union new competences in areas such as climate change and energy policy. these competences are becoming particularly important in the context of the eu's energy dependence on third countries.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, as this is my first speech to this new parliament, i would like to congratulate you on your election as vice-president. as regards the question by mrs weber, i speak on behalf of vice-president barrot and i would first like to thank the rapporteur and the members of the libe committee for the excellent quality of their work. the commission welcomes the report and supports some of the proposed amendments. the commission is generally in favour of the proposal put forward by five member states, although the text is not as ambitious as it would have liked. in particular, the commission regrets that the scope of the framework decision has been limited to cases where the same person is subject to parallel criminal proceedings for the same offence. the commission also regrets that the obligation to refer a case of conflict of jurisdiction to eurojust has been limited and that the list of criteria to be taken into account in determining the best placed court has been removed from the operative part of the text. these amendments have weakened the text of the proposal, removing most of its added value. in the commission's view, the proposal should be seen as merely a first step towards the prevention and resolution of conflicts of jurisdiction in criminal proceedings and should be replaced by a more comprehensive proposal at a later stage. the commission will also consider this in the light of the changes brought about by the lisbon treaty in this area, which i hope will come into force as soon as possible.
rapporteur. − madam president, the positive result of the irish referendum on the lisbon treaty brings us one step closer to that moment in time when the european parliament will not only be consulted by the council, but will have codecision powers on matters which are now under the third pillar. the question then is: why is the council so keen to adopt legislation a few months before that date when, moreover, that legislation does not represent a step forward in establishing a genuine european area of freedom, security and justice? the truth is that this proposal does not help prevent any conflicts of jurisdiction, and does not provide for any settlement when such situations arise. this could be done, for example, by reducing multiple jurisdiction and by allocating jurisdiction to member states, as was done through various regulations on civil law, with the obligation to mutually recognise the decisions that followed from that allocation of jurisdiction. instead, this framework decision is limited to a duty of member states to inform one another and to enter into direct consultation in order to reach ‘consensus on any effective solution aimed at avoiding the adverse consequences arriving from parallel proceedings’. that is why i was not surprised when, during the exchange of views in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs a few weeks ago, the commission – although supporting the current proposal – mentioned it would come up with a new proposal at a later stage. that is also why i am not surprised by what the commissioner has said this evening. i thank the commission for being so honest about the proposal, but have to say that i consider this proposal and the entire procedure for its adoption a good example of how we should not legislate within the european union. i strongly believe that what is important is to protect our citizens’ rights and not just to tick boxes. by the way, the council is not present today, although the presidency was one of the initiators of the proposal. i have to stress that within the european parliament we took our work very seriously. we worked in good faith during the last mandate and this one, and would hope to be sending a message on our views on having more effective legislation. what i welcome about this proposal is that the current text explicitly refers to the principle of ne bis in idem. this was due to the exchange of views we had with the council and the commission, as the original text proposed did not mention it at all. the report i drafted pays particular attention to three aspects. firstly i believe that the protection of persons formally charged must receive the highest attention and consistent procedural safeguards have to be provided for. these should include the right of the formally charged person to receive enough information for him or her to have a basis upon which to challenge any solution which does not appear to be reasonable. secondly, with regard to the details concerning the person formally charged, which national authorities exchange through the notifications, i support the idea that it is important to ensure an adequate level of data protection and that it should be specified in this framework decision what kind of personal data is exchanged. last but not least, i strongly believe that the involvement of eurojust in the decision on the choice of jurisdiction is of the utmost importance. in my opinion, eurojust should be involved from the earliest stage because of its coordinating role and because of its more and more relevant tasks. i am among those who consider that we created this agency not only to show that we are concerned with combating transborder crime, but because we need strong instruments. eurojust has already proved in the years since its establishment that it deserves our trust. that is why i am surprised by the reluctance shown by the council and by some colleagues in the european parliament. having said that, i would like to call on the european commission to present at the earliest opportunity a proposal completing this framework decision on the conflicts of jurisdiction. i will finish by thanking the shadow rapporteurs for the way they worked on this report.
on behalf of the ppe group. – madam president, i would also like to start by thanking the rapporteur for the very good cooperation we have had in this matter. as the shadow rapporteur for the ppe group, i would like to present the ppe position on the framework decision as it is, and of course on the amendments. the ppe position differs from that of the rapporteur on two matters. the first is the degree of involvement of eurojust in direct communication between the domestic authorities. while the rapporteur asks for mandatory involvement of eurojust in every case from the initial stage of communication, we believe that the referral to eurojust should only take place when national authorities fail to reach consensus because, after all, as it is now this initiative is about direct communication. we too would like to strengthen eurojust and its part in the judicial cooperation. our position on this matter only seeks to prevent bureaucracy. if there is a possibility of the two parties reaching consensus, why introduce another body and procedure? we do believe and agree that eurojust must play a role when the parties fail to reach consensus, but where there is not a problem we give the national authorities the flexibility to have direct bilateral contacts, which also boosts public trust. the second matter relates to another proposed amendment which extends the competence of eurojust beyond that provided in article 4 of the eurojust decision. we believe that this matter, if it is to be discussed, should be approached in relation to the eurojust decision via the main door. this is why we will vote against these amendments. however, there are no key points, so we will vote for the report as we want to encourage the exchange of information between national authorities. we also support the oral amendment tabled today. finally i would like to stress that the ppe is keen to see judicial cooperation enhanced, and supports a european policy which should help citizens have the same guarantees and procedures in all member states.
first of all, i would like to congratulate my colleague the rapporteur on her work and to underline that joint action at european level to strengthen freedom, security and justice is essential. i welcome this initiative to resolve conflicts of jurisdiction, because member states often face problems with the mutual recognition of judgments in criminal matters. there must be no differences between member states as regards the protection of accused persons, and we should, in our approach, ensure that anywhere in europe, any accused person can benefit from sound procedural guarantees. in exchanges of information between countries, account should be taken of the need to protect personal data and to clearly establish the nature of data that may be transmitted. i would stress the importance of direct consultations between the authorities of the european union countries, in order to eliminate parallel procedures and to avoid situations where the competent institutions of a given state are subjective in drawing up judgments on the charges brought against a citizen, often for lack of information. we should also propose in the future to strengthen the role of eurojust in resolving possible conflicts and to implement closer cooperation between member states for the benefit of citizens.

i congratulate the rapporteur and the co-rapporteur on their work and welcome the initiative on a framework decision on the prevention and settlement of conflicts of jurisdiction in criminal proceedings. i would like to make an important point: this proposal for a framework decision deals exclusively with positive conflicts of jurisdiction. no provision is made for negative conflicts of jurisdiction. i believe that eurojust's involvement should only follow where the parties do not reach a common agreement. the principle of this directive is to establish direct communication between the competent authorities of the member states. furthermore, it is in the interest of the person concerned that the procedure be as short as possible in order not to be investigated for the same offence in two countries.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, i thank mr simpson and the whole transport committee for bringing such a delicate matter to the attention of parliament. this question allows me to solemnly reiterate what has been said in recent weeks about the inconvenience caused to many european citizens, to many passengers, by the failure of certain airlines. as this parliament knows, the protection of passengers in all areas of transport is a real priority for me. i said that at the hearing when parliament decided to give me its confidence, and i want to say it again tonight. i think we all need to be mobilised in the search for a concrete regulatory solution, also to avoid - as president simpson has argued - the disparity between a passenger who has bought a simple airline ticket from a company which then goes bankrupt and a passenger who has bought it as part of a wider package holiday. i think the first thing to do is to use the instruments we already have. so all regulations, even if they are incomplete and even if they cause disparities, must in any case be used in the best way by citizens. in order to optimise the instruments at our disposal, the network of european consumer protection centres was set up to advise consumers on their rights and to collect complaints, for example, in the event of the bankruptcy of sky europe. but we also need to protect passengers better when they are faced with a failure. passengers with reservations that expire should be entitled to a refund and, in some cases, repatriation. it is a complex problem, which requires us to consider carefully the measures to be taken. the commission has already started work on a concrete response to these questions. at our request, an important study has already been carried out on the consequences of failures in the air transport sector, especially as regards passengers. it is a detailed study, which gives a concrete picture of the consequences of failures and their impact on over 700 million passengers transported each year throughout the european union. the study presents several possible scenarios for defining the most appropriate solutions to the various problems raised by bankruptcies, in particular in terms of reimbursement and repatriation, as mentioned earlier. this has enabled various scenarios to be worked out for both reimbursement and repatriation, ranging from the setting up of guarantee funds, to the development of compulsory insurance schemes for passengers or airlines, and finally to the hypothesis of introducing targeted changes in national insolvency rights. in february of this year i handed the study to mr costa, then chairman of the tran committee. on the basis of this study, the commission is now continuing its analysis of the various possible options, focusing in particular on the impact on consumers and the air transport sector. in the course of the analysis we will take account of all elements of the debate and will use the input of all interested parties. in this connection, the commission will launch a wide public consultation on air passenger rights in the coming weeks. in this context, and without underestimating the differences and specificities of all-inclusive travel, the commission will also take account of the impact assessment currently under way on the revision of directive 90/314 on all-inclusive travel. this is because one of the main objectives of the public consultation will be precisely to define the consequences of airline failures for passengers and possible solutions to remedy them. of course, in addition to the public consultation, there will be a study to analyse the impact of the various possible solutions. of course, parliament's contribution will be decisive for me and - given the commitment with which the committee on transport has mobilised today with this oral question - i believe that in the coming weeks we will be able to cooperate fruitfully in order to identify together the most appropriate solution to meet the needs of passengers and to ensure, in the best possible way, their rights in the event of the bankruptcy of airlines.
on behalf of the epp group. in the context of the global economic crisis, fluctuating fuel prices and increasing competition, airlines, especially low-cost carriers, are facing major difficulties. increasing ticket prices is not an option in the current situation, and the increase in fares by some low-cost carriers may lead to an even sharper decline in passenger numbers. the financial losses of airlines in 2009 will be approximately $11 billion, and the situation will not recover until the next three years. in this context, though unwelcome, there is the situation where airlines go bankrupt. in the event of bankruptcy due to the lack of adequate legislation, there is no practical way to recover the countervalue of tickets or to obtain the repatriation of passengers left outside their country of residence. the counter-cost, albeit modest, support provided by european airlines to the passengers of a company in bankruptcy, as demonstrated in the sky europe case, although meritorious in itself, offers only a temporary solution to overcome a one-off crisis. on the other hand, the economic crisis itself cannot be considered as a permanent excuse, since airline failures have already occurred before the crisis. tighter controls on the financial position of air carriers, especially low-cost carriers, tighter controls on mergers and takeovers, and the establishment of a strong guarantee fund are some of the solutions that could, in the long term, provide protection for passengers in the event of an airline's bankruptcy.
an effective internal market requires a consumer protection policy at community level. over the years, the european union has acted and taken measures to increase consumer safety in areas such as package holidays and travellers' rights. however, a large majority of complaints received from european consumers relate to the non-respect of air passenger rights. the commission notes that the airport services agreement concluded between ryanair and ams was signed on 29 june 2012 and entered into force on 1 january 2013. in these cases, for consumers, problems arise when the flight is not operated as planned. although the european union's council directive 90/314 on package holidays protects passengers in the event of the insolvency of the tour operator, it does not protect them in the case of airline tickets sold individually. in addition, in the event of denied boarding, compensation is excluded in the event of extraordinary circumstances, including the bankruptcy of the airlines. according to a recent study, the number of bankruptcies of air carriers in the european union for the period 2000-2008 amounted to 79. the commission notes that the airport services agreement concluded between ryanair and ams was signed on 29 june 2010 and entered into force on 1 january 2010. so how can we do better to protect passengers in such situations? perhaps a system of passenger insurance to cover these situations, a more rigorous system of supervision, the development of legislative provisions to ensure compensation for passengers in such situations.

the idea of a european society dates back to the 1950s and was taken up again after the entry into force of the treaty of rome, as part of the common market objective. the current status of the european company has symbolic value, of a european enterprise and enjoys a certain freedom of establishment and mobility. many companies use the european company status to show their uniqueness as european, and it is also an essential tool for companies looking to develop their cross-border merger strategies. one of the main advantages of a european company is that its registered office can be transferred from the member state in which it was incorporated to another member state without the need to dissolve the company or create a new legal entity. however, european society is far from the initial objectives of an autonomous status governed by a single legislation. the practical functioning is therefore deficient. legislation is not uniform and depends on the particularities of national legislation, and the mobility of a european company is restricted by provisions prohibiting the establishment of a registered office or a head office in different member states. one of the community's fundamental freedoms is thus restricted, namely the freedom of movement of companies. the european commission's report on the application of the regulation, which the commissioner mentioned, i think will have to include a study on the possibility of having the head office and registered office of a european company in different member states and will have to consider a revision of the regulation to go further towards creating an autonomous statute for this type of company.

in writing. − improving judicial cooperation in criminal proceedings between authorities exercising parallel competences is particularly important. where the facts giving rise to the commission of an offence fall within the jurisdiction of two or more member states, it is necessary that criminal proceedings be conducted in the most appropriate jurisdiction and the establishment of a common and uniform framework for the choice of that jurisdiction in an objective and transparent manner is essential. the ineffective application of the principle of ne bis in idem, which is contained in the convention implementing the schengen agreement, leads to a violation of fundamental rights and is contrary to the eu's objective of creating a common area of freedom, security and justice. the report we voted for supports the principle of ensuring that this principle is respected throughout the european judicial area and not just in national proceedings, which is why i welcome its adoption at yesterday's sitting.
