on behalf of the s&d group. the creation of an evaluation and monitoring mechanism to verify the application of the schengen acquis is an important measure to put into practice the decisions on the area of freedom, security and justice, in particular the provisions of the hague programme. the proposals for today's debate are a variant of an evaluation mechanism. they shall contain provisions specific to the field concerned and an appropriate control methodology. a closer look, however, reveals a lack of respect for the principles of interinstitutional cooperation, both at the level of the european union and between the member states of the union. in this respect, the proposal contains provisions which limit cooperation between member states in evaluating the results of the application of the schengen agreement and, at the same time, unduly increase the role of the commission in this process, while keeping the european parliament out of the whole evaluation mechanism. moreover, the wording of certain articles of the regulation leaves room for different interpretations of the relationship between the commission, parliament and the council as regards their access to information on the application of the schengen acquis. article 14 of the regulation, which concerns sensitive information, thus states that 'reports drawn up after on-the-spot visits are classified as restricted documents. the commission, after consulting the member state concerned, shall decide which part of the report may be made public. in connection with these provisions, i would point out that it does not follow from article 16, which refers to the report to the european parliament and the council, that the annual report on the evaluations carried out will also contain information with restricted regulation on the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster. ladies and gentlemen, freedom, security and justice are areas of the utmost support mr coelho's proposal that this draft, as it stands, should be rejected and returned to the commission. i propose that we support the motion.

we live on a planet characterized by a diversity of climatic environments. but there is one single element that affects all of this: climate change. the reality is that the effects of these changes are transnational and affect us all in different ways, whether it is floods, droughts, fires or devastating storms. the main cause of these disasters is evidently the uncontrolled development of certain categories of activities, resulting in increased carbon dioxide emissions and global warming. current statistics show that the per capita carbon dioxide emissions of developed countries can be hundreds of times higher than those of developing countries. given this reality, i feel compelled to ask a rhetorical question: is it our duty to support developing countries with initiatives and technologies that keep a clean planet? i think the answer is obvious, and taking action does not allow for any hesitation for us and future generations.
development and cooperation mechanisms, as well as the allocation of a substantial climate change fund to developing countries, are important for the conclusion of a post-kyoto international agreement. however, the best argument for persuading other states to join a post-kyoto agreement is the measures the european union is taking to meet its commitments already made. for non-ets sectors, the measures envisaged may include: renovation of energy-inefficient buildings, establishment of an energy efficiency fund in each member state, significant increase of the erdf share that can be used for energy efficiency in housing and development of public transport. these measures can create around 7 million jobs at european level by 2020. for ets sectors, financing mechanisms for the low carbon economy are needed. the re-engineering of european energy or metallurgical companies will enable them to produce in an environmentally friendly way.
in writing. we need to look at the costs of the clean energy transition not as an economic burden that will lead to higher production costs for companies and higher public spending in national budgets, but as investments that will bring tangible benefits in terms of jobs, technological innovation, clean infrastructure, and contribute to the sustainable development of the countries concerned. climate change is a threat to the balance of our environment and our habitat. europe must show courage and be consistent in its leadership in the effort to combat global warming. in the interests of fairness and historical responsibility, poor countries must be helped to strengthen and adapt their economies to new challenges, while protecting themselves from the effects of global warming to which they are most vulnerable. i hope that those attending the december conference will understand that there is no alternative to reducing emissions and that a delayed decision in copenhagen on binding targets will mean a failure not only of the conference but also of multilateral dialogue on global issues that affect our future, the future of all of us.
in writing. climate change is one of the most serious environmental, social and economic threats. crop productivity fluctuates from year to year and is significantly influenced by the variability of extreme climatic conditions. it affects all sectors of the economy, but agriculture remains the most vulnerable. i believe that this problem must be tackled in two aspects: - an action plan in the worst affected areas: the use of plant varieties resistant to the new climatic parameters, the adaptation of the agricultural calendar to the new conditions, afforestation, the construction of greenhouses, the management of agricultural water resources, the greening of polluted land; - the other aspect must be a forward-looking plan to eliminate the causes of climate change by promoting a low-carbon global economy, coupled with a promotion of energy security. i also believe that it is important to develop strategies for preventing and managing natural disasters, because over the last decade droughts and floods have occurred frequently, with a negative impact on both agricultural production and flora and fauna. i firmly believe that the european union must maintain its leadership in the fight against climate change, which must not be put in second place because of the current economic difficulties.
in writing. achieving an agreement in copenhagen will provide the necessary impetus for coordinating global action to combat climate change. the climate crisis must be linked to the economic crisis: it is the opportunity to move from an unsustainable economy based on limited natural resources to a sustainable economy. in addition to promoting the strategy of energy security and energy efficiency, europe needs to develop its investment plan in new energy technologies. promoting green technologies at community level involves not only finding an alternative to the energy crisis, but also boosting economic growth and job creation. on the other hand, the copenhagen agreement provides an opportunity to promote future links between the eu emissions trading system and regional or federal trading systems in the us and other countries that practice this type of system or similar systems. last but not least, the eu must take a united stance to maintain its leadership role in the negotiations and must actively participate in strengthening existing climate partnerships with developing countries and in forging new partnerships where they do not yet exist.
in writing. over the next 50 years, climate change will have significant effects on important economic sectors such as agriculture, energy, transport, ecosystems, tourism and health. climate change will also affect households, businesses and certain sectors of society, in particular the elderly, people with disabilities and low-income households. the eu is determined to act swiftly to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. but mitigating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions is not enough. mitigation requires a complementary short-term response. the effects of climate change are expected to be more significant than anticipated and will occur regardless of the mitigation measures that will be implemented. this is why measures are needed to strengthen the resilience of natural and human systems to cope with the impacts of climate change, i.e. adaptation policies. these policies are under way in the eu, but they are also needed globally, and that is why the copenhagen conference must be an international success. we need a global solidarity pact to develop green economies by promoting clean technologies that secure jobs and protect the environment and public health.
in writing. – the negotiations in copenhagen on financing to developing countries will be crucial if this summit is to be successful. already, some african countries have said they will not be able to commit to the kind of deal we need at copenhagen if it does not contain suitable measures for financing of mitigation and adaptation in developing countries. there are two key points here - the first is that the public money given to these developing countries must be new, additional money and should not come from existing aid budgets. the second point is that it isn't just public money which can be used in this context; in addition to directly providing aid, steps can be taken to encourage private sector investment in low carbon economies. the extent to which the private sector is prepared to invest in developing countries will depend on international agreements on emission trading schemes. agreements on this issue will provide the policy coherence and stability which give the private sector the confidence to invest properly in developing countries. the negotiations must therefore aim for both comprehensive commitments regarding public financing and concrete measures to secure private sector investment.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. i fully support the european community's accession to the statute of the international renewable energy agency (irena). the main objective of this is to disseminate good practice in the field of renewable energy, both within the european union and globally. under its statute, the agency will promote and support the use of renewable resources globally. by acceding to the status of this agency, the community will enjoy better direct access to information on renewable energy activities, both at european and global level. the commission will also be able to monitor the progress of member states towards the mandatory 2020 target for renewable energy.
in writing. − in voting for this report, i want to stress the importance of establishing this international organisation, which will promote and support the use of renewable resources across the globe, given the benefits that can be gained from their contribution to environmental and climate protection, economic growth and social cohesion, including poverty reduction, energy security and regional development. at the bonn conference in january 2009, romania, the first signatory country, was appointed vice-chair of this first meeting and was also admitted to the irena administrative committee, the nucleus that provides the agency's interim secretariat until it starts to function. today, 137 countries, including 24 eu member states, have signed the statute.
in writing. − the coordination of certain laws and administrative provisions of the member states concerning the broadcasting of television programmes is essential for the creation of a media space characterised by unity in diversity. equally important is our ability to make european legislation as accessible as possible to all citizens. the report on the proposal for an audiovisual media services directive in its codified version, which has been tabled before the house, is a purely technical and legal measure, but its benefits are undeniable. codifying legislation that is constantly changing is a way of bringing more clarity and transparency to community law, making it more understandable to eu citizens. in the present case, the proposed codification consists in replacing the old 1989 directive with a new directive (without any changes in content), to which the acts which have supplemented it over time have been added. i supported this initiative because, beyond its technical nature, its value for the smooth functioning of audiovisual media services, but also in terms of transparency, cannot be overlooked.
in writing. − i agree with the text of this report because information pluralism should be a fundamental principle of the european union. diversification of the mass media means a multiplication of views, and this is essential in a democratic society. in addition, there is an economic component to this argument: traditional audiovisual media services (such as television) and newly emerging ones (e.g. 'video on demand') provide important employment opportunities in europe, especially in small and medium-sized enterprises, which stimulate economic growth and investment.
in writing. − the creation of the schengen area by the abolition of internal border controls and the introduction of freedom of movement within the union is one of the european union's most important achievements. given the permeability of borders, we need high standards in the practical application of the schengen acquis in order to maintain a high level of mutual trust between member states and in their ability to implement the measures accompanying the abolition of internal border controls. the evaluation mechanism for monitoring the application of the schengen acquis needs to be improved. the need to maintain a high level of security and trust requires good cooperation between the governments of the member states and the commission. given the importance of this legislative initiative and its relevance from the point of view of fundamental rights and freedoms, it is regrettable that the european parliament is in the position of consultant and not of co-legislator as it should have been. that is why i voted against the commission's legislative proposal.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. − madam president, compared to the 2009 budget, the commission proposal for 2010 provides for a moderate increase on the budget lines concerning internal market and customs policy, whereas the amount of money allocated to consumer policy remains stable. in the draft 2010 budget the council has decreased the money, in particular for budget lines which concern the development of the internal market. i believe that a functioning internal market in these times of economic crisis can contribute to the economic recovery. in the area of customs policy, the budget will assure cooperation and coordination measures, thus reinforcing security and protection of external borders, supporting the fight against illicit trafficking and fraud as well as improving the efficiency of customs systems. i consider measures in the area of consumer education a priority, in particular the strengthening of financial literacy. the crisis has shown how important consumer policy, in particular consumer education, is in order to help consumers to take responsible economic decisions. for all these reasons, the imco committee called for a separate budget line on the solvit programme to be financed by an amount of eur 1 million. solvit is a very good example of how you can help businesses and citizens. finally, for the continuation of the pilot project monitoring measures in the field of consumer policy for the consolidation of a scoreboard and related market study, as a preparatory action, the amount adopted is eur 1 million.
in writing. drafting a budget is never an easy process, especially in times of economic crisis, but its importance is all the greater for this reason. the management of a crisis of the magnitude of the present one depends on the european level and on the balance that is found in the negotiations between the competent european institutions. the role of the ep is undoubtedly crucial in this debate. the 2010 budget discussions focused on the economic recovery plan and the european milk fund. in a way, they demonstrated the rigidity of the 2007-2013 financial framework, representing new financial projects and therefore new money. the european budget needs to use all its financial margins to respond to the economic crisis. however, this budget risks having a limited impact if member states do not take an active stance in accessing the available funds. we need to send a strong message to european capitals and, in my case, to bucharest in particular: our work here to get more money for european funds is useless if those responsible at home do not take the necessary steps to access and use them effectively.
in writing. – i welcome the proposal of the draft budget for 2010 as it is a balanced report, taking into consideration in a realistic manner the eu’s priorities. two matters are to be highlighted – the increases to payments on the main lines (erdf, esf, cohesion fund) for regional development, and the creation of a ‘milk fund’. the increases to payments are important as they will boost the implementation of structural policy in the member states for the benefit of all european citizens, while the setting-up of a special ‘milk fund’ would represent a strong signal sent out by the european institutions to european farmers. a third key point in the budget is represented by energy policy, an essential area for 2010 as it will be the year of the adoption of a new energy plan for the period 2010-2014 aimed at boosting the eu’s energy security and competitiveness. in the coming years the commission should also consider as a priority investments in infrastructure, especially in the new member states, as they have a positive effect on economic and territorial cohesion.
in writing. the establishment of the dairy fund would send an important signal to european farmers that the eu institutions are genuinely concerned about the dairy crisis. the milk market is one of the most volatile markets and has been severely affected by the economic crisis we are going through. such a substantive solution - the establishment of a fund to support the modernisation of the sector - is clearly preferable to palliative solutions such as a return to traditional means of regulating production through milk quotas. we would all have liked a larger financial allocation, but the amount proposed for the creation of this fund, eur 300 million, is the maximum amount compatible with the budgetary ceiling - any exceeding of this ceiling would have made it impossible for the council of ministers to approve the establishment of the fund. at the same time, new approaches are needed to boost the use of rural development funds by livestock farmers. i believe that the most useful approaches would be those relating to access to information, exchange of good practice and training on how to claim these funds, which are currently underused in some member states.
member of the commission. − i think that again you have pointed to a very important problem. we already discussed this morning that we now have 78 million people in the european union with basic or lower skills, and it is very clear that, by the deadline which we have set for ourselves of 2020, we will definitely not have the same number of jobs for the people with basic or lower skills. therefore it is absolutely imperative to prepare for that time: we have to upgrade and modernise our educational system, and we have to progress with analysing and searching to ascertain what these new skills and jobs might be. we have to prepare the younger generation in particular, but also the middle generation, for this. therefore we would like to continue with the ongoing research under the strategic framework ‘education and training 2020’ for policy cooperation and mutual learning. this is just one of the frameworks in which we would like to continue and to cooperate with educational institutions and with businesses on future requirements for the most wide-ranging and most relevant mix of skills that our citizens will need by 2020.
member of the commission. − you started your question with a very clear analysis that there is a division of labour and division of competences, but it is very clear that the commission is strongly behind all efforts to increase the proportion of the population with the highest possible level of education. it is very clear that only by improving the level of education, by enlarging access to high-quality tertiary education, as you mentioned, that we can preserve the cutting edge of the european economy and preserve the prosperity and high living standards we enjoy in europe. i think therefore that the commission and the member states have to work very closely in this respect to create the conditions whereby students or pupils from difficult socioeconomic backgrounds can also get a fair chance and fair access to higher and university education.
today, 19 percent of young europeans drop out of school. the european union cannot have sustainable economic development if it fails to invest in education and research. only five member states have so far invested more than 2% of their gross domestic product in research and innovation. the economic crisis has reduced both the gross domestic product of the member states and the community budget. there is therefore a risk that budgets for education and research will be reduced in the coming years. for the european union to remain economically competitive and create new jobs, we need to invest in education and innovation. what steps can the commission, together with the member states, take to ensure that the minimum level of investment in research and education is secured in the years ahead?
member of the commission. − you are absolutely right that the percentage of early school leavers in europe is very high. we set ourselves the level of 10% to achieve by 2010; it is quite obvious that this benchmark will not be reached, because currently there are around 15% of early school leavers, and you are absolutely right that this does not reflect well on the need for quality in our educational systems around europe. you are also right that, under current circumstances – where national governments are under different constraints regarding public finances and the financing of stimulus packages, and are very often implementing exit strategies aimed at restoring public finances to a sound footing in the coming years – there is much debate over the budget. what should be the priorities? where should we place our emphasis? i think you have already noticed that there is always a strong voice from the commission side highlighting the need to keep an adequate level of financing for research and innovation in the educational sectors, because we believe this is how we will preserve and improve our competitive edge and prepare our future researchers, our future workers in highly competitive areas for better performance in the future. you will certainly hear voices from the commission appealing clearly to keep financing for education-related activities and for research and innovatory aid at the highest possible level, even under these very difficult economic constraints.
member of the commission. − mr president, i already used some of the arguments in my previous answer, but it is clear that this is a very important area and i will try to highlight some other additional information in responding to this question. as you know, in accordance with articles 149 and 150 of the ec treaty, responsibility for the content and organisation of education and training systems rests with the member states. it is really up to them to decide the content of their educational programmes for all levels of education and training. the commission recognises, however, the importance of the issue raised by the honourable member and supports member states in implementing their reforms through the open method of coordination. the 2006 recommendation on key competences for lifelong learning defines the key competences young people should develop during their initial education and training to a level that equips them for adult life and which would allow them to develop very good job skills for the future. we should also look at the aforementioned strategic framework for european cooperation in education and training (‘et 2020’) from this perspective. i would underline that among the priority areas for the first cycle of this programme, the commission aims to develop cooperation among member states on improving basic skills in reading, mathematics and science, and to intensify work on reducing the number of early leavers from education and training. through the copenhagen process, european union member states are increasingly cooperating to share experience and improve links between vocational education and training and the labour market to help youngsters access the labour market on better terms. boosting the attractiveness and quality of vocational educational training is a main priority, as is fostering the notion of lifelong learning and related policies so that the european workforce is flexible and able to adapt to changes in labour market conditions. just to highlight some other programmes, the leonardo da vinci programme’s mobility action is also a highly effective tool to help youngsters access the labour market. this mostly concerns apprentices and other youngsters on the job market. thanks to this programme, they can undertake part of their training in another country. so far, the results have been very positive because these placements abroad have improved skills that are useful for employers. they have improved their language abilities and intercultural skills. i should also mention the erasmus programme, but in a slightly different light because up to now we have been speaking mostly about exchanges for students among universities. since 2007, however, the erasmus programme has also been supporting student placements in enterprises. this programme has been very successful since the start, as in its first year of operation alone over 20 000 students carried out a work placement abroad and over 15 000 enterprises have participated in this effort. this is one example of how we can enhance the employability of graduates and foster better cooperation between academia and business. we have already discussed the positive impact of the bologna process on student mobility and on cooperation among universities and higher education institutions, so i will not repeat what i already said a few minutes ago. to conclude, i would like to underline that the commission acknowledges the particular difficulties that young people face when they are entering the labour market. in the framework of the lisbon strategy for growth and more and better jobs, both the commission and the european council have put a particular focus on improving the employment situation of young people. member states have committed themselves through the adoption of the european youth pact in 2005 to devote more attention to the integration of young people into education, employment and society overall, but the initial very promising progress has been stalled because of the current economic crisis. it is true that young people have been hit particularly hard as they have been the first to lose their jobs under the current circumstances. in its communication ‘a shared commitment for employment’ of june 2009, the commission has encouraged member states and social partners to ensure that young people, despite the difficult economic environment, have access to quality education and training and, in particular, to high-quality apprenticeships and traineeships.
the economic crisis risks making it harder for young people to find work, accepting work below their level of qualification or being forced to go through longer periods of unemployment. the commission should ensure that they will have the opportunity to train during this period of unemployment and not be disadvantaged by employment conditions requiring a minimum period of experience, sometimes 5-10 years. what measures does the commission envisage to this end?

there are voices in this parliament who, whatever the subject is, have the same subject they are dealing with and sometimes not as they should. it is clear that the european council must first find a solution for the czech republic to complete the procedures for ratifying the treaty of lisbon. this solution must be fair to all the other member states. at the same time, we must not forget the economic crisis we are still facing and for which immediate solutions must also be found. the economic and financial crisis and the exceptional financial measures taken over the past year have destabilised public finances in most eu countries to a worrying degree. so far, 17 of the 27 member states are under the commission's excessive deficit watch, and estimates suggest that another three will soon be in the same situation. regardless of economic strength, member states exceeded their assumptions, as the crisis led to a sharp decline in budget revenues and an above-planned increase in public expenditure. it is true that there are clear indications of an economic recovery in the near future and that is why we can begin to talk about reducing financial incentives in certain areas. however, the specific situation of each member state must be taken into account and the european institutions must recognise that we are not yet at the stage where we can completely abandon public support for all economic sectors. member states need to agree on the continuation of the exit strategy and the right tools for doing so, including the intensification of structural reforms that can reduce the fiscal deficit in the medium term and naturally contribute to economic recovery. inadequate management of the post-crisis period by member states may destabilise the internal market of the european union. the continuation of public support must therefore be decided and permitted according to the particular conditions in each state.

madam president, the transatlantic relations that are crucial for both the eu and the us have been seriously tested in recent years. now, with a new administration in the white house which is redefining us priorities, and france back into the nato military structure, the perspective is better. personally i consider that the time is now ripe for a substantive evaluation of transatlantic relations to give them the solid basis they deserve to withstand the current common challenges posed by the international environment – energy, climate change, emerging new powers, the financial and economic crisis, and terrorism. this time we should go beyond superficial policy differences and evaluate our deeper common interests which, until now, have simply been taken for granted. the truth is that, without such a profound joint evaluation, we in the west could lose the initiative to other centres of power, who will not hesitate to shape the world according to their interests – not ours. security in europe, for instance, is one such common interest and therefore stands at the heart of transatlantic relations. even if, for now, war on the continent is not a serious proposition, the culmination of some current negative trends could bring back that possibility if we fail to respond properly. progress is not irreversible, as we all know so well in central europe. that is why, before considering a proposal to re-evaluate the current security architecture of the continent, we should try to have definite answers as to the continuation of us involvement, the future of nato and the role expected of the eu after the lisbon treaty comes into force. if europe wants to realise its ambition to be a true player in world politics, it should eliminate such differences between its members, thus trying to motivate them equally around true common economic interests.
acting president of the council. - madam president! - what is it? i thank all members for their contributions to this debate. there is a broad consensus on the importance of deepening cooperation with the us administration and the summit we are about to hold. it is gratifying that the american government is showing such a willingness to deepen and develop our relations. i think we have a lot of good things going on and we are well prepared to take some important steps. we have a number of common problems with our partner the united states and it is therefore urgent to find common solutions. i believe that we can make progress on the climate issue, the economic crisis and the doha round - reaffirming the importance of its conclusion - and that we can initiate extremely important processes in the legal field. the economic partnership is a very important forum for us. we also see the importance of discussing important regional issues, such as afghanistan, pakistan and the middle east. i was asked some specific questions. the commission is also proposing to extend the visa-free regime to all eu countries. it is unfortunate that this is not the case today, but we continue to work very intensively to make this a reality. as regards the so-called tobin tax, i know that there are members of parliament who are ardent supporters of it. i would like to put it this way: a tobin tax can only work if it is global and if there are global control instruments - otherwise it becomes another protectionist measure. there are no conditions at present for an international, global agreement on a tobin tax, so the presidency will not pursue this issue. i want to be clear about that. with regard to swift, we agree with the united states on the importance of being able to exchange information on financial transfers. it is valuable in the fight against cross-border crime and terrorism. now a new agreement is needed because the belgian company swift is moving to europe, but we are both keen to keep the programme to prevent the financing of terrorism. in a transitional phase we need to find an agreement that can be applied for a short time until we have the new lisbon treaty in place. there have been experts who have looked at this, including the french judge jean-louis bruguyère who, on behalf of the eu, inspected tftp. he believes that the legal certainty and data protection requirements of the current agreement are adequate. the more permanent agreement will also eventually, when the treaty of lisbon has entered into force, provide for the european parliament to be actively involved in its formulation. it is a very important meeting we are facing next week, but it is after all just a meeting. i believe that we can move forward, resolve certain issues and initiate important processes on the issues that we have in common and need to resolve in close and strategic partnership with the us government. i am very pleased to see the strong support in the european parliament for the council and the commission in our efforts. i will of course report on the results of this next time we meet in the brussels plenary.

this was mentioned, that the energy council will not overlap with the tec. the agendas will complement each other. it is clear that security issues will go to the energy council, whereas regulatory issues go to the tech. the focus of the energy council is on new technologies and energy security. a very brief word on swift and some gls questions that have been mentioned. the swift agreement is agreement is at the heart of the swift agreement, and any us request is subject to the authorisation of an eu judicial authority within that framework, so we have to keep working on it. on the esta, consular instructions. we will, however, prepare a final assessment once the final rule on esta has been published, and this evaluation will also address the question of the esta fee if the fee is acting president of the council. - the council recalls that the free movement of persons is one of the fundamental rights guaranteed by community law, including the right of eu citizens to live and work in another member state. at its meeting on 9 march 2009, the council addressed an invitation to those member states which still apply transitional rules restricting free movement. the council then said that in the light of the facts available, the continued application of restrictions should be considered. the countries were also invited to lift the restrictions during the third phase if no serious disturbances, or any risk of serious disturbances, could be detected in the labour markets of the member states concerned. the council also stressed to the member states the need to give priority to nationals of member states over non-eu workers and that the protection of nationals of new member states who were already resident and employed in a member state would be maintained during transitional periods. in addition, the rights of family members have been taken into account in accordance with the practice of previous accessions. the council stressed the strong elements of differentiation and flexibility in the rules on the free movement of workers. member states have declared that they will seek to grant increased access to the labour market for nationals of the new member states concerned under national law, with a view to accelerating the approximation to the acquis communautaire. in november 2008, the commission presented its communication on the consequences of the free movement of workers after enlargement. the commission notes that workers from bulgaria, romania and the eu-10 member states have contributed to meeting an increased demand for labour in the beneficiary countries, thereby significantly supporting continued economic growth. the available data suggest that post-enlargement mobility within the eu has not led to and will not lead to any serious disruption of the labour market. the commission also notes that it is labour supply and demand, rather than rules restricting access to the labour market, that govern the extent and direction of intra-eu mobility. the commission concludes that the restrictions applied by the member states may lead to a longer adjustment period in the labour market and an increase in the proportion of undeclared work. the free movement of labour is a key priority for the european union. labour mobility contributes to more jobs, to the ability of the economy to adapt even in the event of an economic crisis. moreover, the mobility of workers contributes to reducing social exclusion and poverty. as regards the transitional period for free movement requested by the honourable member, member states are entitled to maintain their restrictions until the end of the third phase of the transitional period. however, the council considers that the economic crisis in europe should not be used as a reason for continuing to apply the transitional rules. even in times of low labour demand, employers may find it difficult to fill vacancies with jobseekers from their own country. the council shall regularly review the question of transitional arrangements. this was most recently done at the june 2009 meeting, when the council took note of the commission's information on the consequences of free movement after enlargement. the commission informed the council that three of the eu-15 member states had notified the commission of serious labour market disturbances or risks thereof before 1 may 2009. germany and austria continued to apply restrictions on labour market entry by maintaining the work permit requirement, while the uk applies a system of ex post registration which allows workers to start employment but requires registration within 30 days. in its information to the council, the commission also stated that it would ensure compliance with the provisions of the accession treaty and reserved the right to request clarifications from those member states which continued to apply restrictions.
i would like to ask you whether you have in your agenda for the swedish presidency an action in your calendar to try to persuade those member states which still maintain these barriers to the free movement of labour to lift them. a second question is whether you will include such a suggestion to lift barriers to the free movement of labour in the swedish presidency conclusions.
member of the commission. − the repeated elections in the republic of moldova on 29 july were a decisive test of the country's ability to consolidate its democratic development and continue on its path towards the european union. we are pleased that the elections took place in a calm and orderly atmosphere and that the new government has not only expressed its firm intention to favour a pro-european orientation but has already taken a number of steps in this direction. on the other hand, the new authorities in the republic of moldova are facing enormous difficulties. one of the most serious crises, one of the greatest difficulties is the need to cope with the consequences of the economic and financial crisis. of the european union's eastern neighbours, the republic of moldova is perhaps the most economically fragile. trade and industrial production have collapsed amid the crisis, as well as the political turmoil generated by the parliamentary elections in april. transfers by moldovan citizens from abroad, which until last year accounted for over a third of the country's gross domestic product, have fallen well below the usual level. exports and imports have fallen dramatically. so is domestic demand and industrial production. a sharp decline, even of more than 10% of gross domestic product, is forecast for 2009. given that moldova is already the poorest country in europe, this setback is particularly painful and will further accentuate the hardships faced by the population and, in particular, the most vulnerable. in order to come to the aid of the republic of moldova and its people, the european union stands ready to support the country by providing macro-financial assistance in addition to that which may be provided by and in coordination with the international monetary fund. we will also provide specialized assistance and accelerate the disbursement of our regular aid to this country. as regards macro-financial assistance, as required for this type of assistance, our support will be conditional on the conclusion of an agreement on a support programme between the republic of moldova and the international monetary fund. the imf representatives are currently in chisinau and we are eagerly awaiting their report. we cannot move forward with the preparation of a macro-financial assistance programme before the launch of the programme with the imf. as such, it is too early to know what form the macro-financial assistance programme that the european commission might grant will take. we expect the authorities to ask for support, not only to strengthen foreign exchange reserves, but also to cover the budget deficit. it should be noted that the republic of moldova is eligible for both grants and loans. what this assistance will ultimately consist of depends, of course, on the needs that will be identified. in the meantime, the european commission has already sent a mission of experts to chisinau, led by the directorate-general for economic and financial affairs dg ecfin, to assist the moldovan authorities in drawing up their economic programme. the objective of the mission, at its recent meeting with the chisinau authorities, was to help them assess the country's reaction to the current economic situation. the commission services used this opportunity to gather the information necessary for the preparation of a macro-financial assistance programme. the commission remains ready to continue to provide the chisinau authorities with expert advice in this area. we are also working to accelerate payments for budget support operations under the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument. in september, the european commission approved an increase in the ceiling for payments for budget support this year from €30.5 million to €34.5 million. of course, the purpose of our assistance, in the form of budget support, is primarily to encourage reforms in the agreed sectors, not just to fill budget gaps. but in the present situation it is not just a means of supplementing limited budgetary resources. it is also a way of helping to overcome the real difficulties faced by the people of the republic of moldova. we particularly welcome the fact that members of the european parliament have requested urgent support for the republic of moldova and in the coming months we will be calling on you to support our efforts in this regard. we are confident that parliament will swiftly approve the macro-financial assistance package for the republic of moldova when it is presented to it. this will ensure that assistance is provided in a timely manner. before concluding, ladies and gentlemen, this statement, allow me to refer briefly to the situation in transnistria. first of all, to underline how important it is not to lose sight of this issue in the context of the significant political changes taking place in the republic of moldova. the talks for the settlement of the conflict should be resumed as soon as possible in the so-called 5+2 format. we are optimistic about this because the new government has reaffirmed support for this principle in its programme. the european union is playing an increasingly important role in this process. we are counting on the new leadership in chisinau to proactively address this issue, which will help to resolve the conflict. for our part, we have just launched two packages of confidence-building projects, with funding from the european commission in the areas of health, environmental, social and economic protection. this action is part of a broader framework of our ongoing efforts to resolve the conflict. ladies and gentlemen, politically, as well as economically, the republic of moldova is at a crossroads. we are fully committed to supporting the country's future development and will continue to do our utmost to ensure that, at this critical juncture, our support is substantial, effective and timely.

in writing. implementing legislation on the marketing of emission allowances involves costs that will be distributed differently in each country, depending on the economic structure of that country. some countries already have a wider range of options that allow them to reduce emissions without significantly increasing energy prices. countries still undergoing energy sector restructuring would feel the impact of these measures disproportionately at the consumer level, relative to the ability to bear the costs of the changes. a country that has a large contribution of wind energy in its energy mix has allowed itself to invest in renewable energy, as it has already developed by polluting. on the other hand, a country that still relies heavily on coal-fired power generation has a technological gap that it needs to close and, at the same time, reduce its emissions. eastern european countries are in this latter situation. for this reason, i believe that the decision on financing climate change must take this into account and exclude the countries of the latest waves of accession from paying contributions that would place an undue burden on these economies.

in writing. unilateral eu action, although a leader in tackling climate change, is not enough. a global agreement on climate change mitigation and adaptation will not be possible without the involvement of developing countries, especially the most advanced. the effects of climate change are already affecting the development of these countries: droughts, floods, natural disasters, desertification, with all its economic and social consequences. all mitigation and adaptation actions require a robust measurement, reporting and verification mechanism, as well as a well-managed public and private funding pool. these joint efforts will contribute to the achievement of the targets of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, developing a sustainable economy and creating green jobs.

the commission on 22 july, is based on article 165 of the treaty. the article refers to the coordination of research and technological development activities between the community and the member states, with the specific aim of ensuring greater coherence between the policies of the member states and those of the community. article 165 and the objectives of the joint programming initiatives are in line. they are based on our joint identification of the challenges facing our societies collectively and our ability to agree on common or coordinated responses to these challenges through increased political commitment by member states. the aim is, of course, to increase the efficiency of public research funding in europe. but i think the problem and the heart of your question is that policies. there is no other legal basis in the treaty under the heading of research on which the commission could base its proposals for action on joint programming initiatives. there is of course a on behalf of the epp group. the swedish presidency intends to adopt conclusions on measures to combat neurodegenerative diseases in december without waiting for the opinion of parliament on this issue. i was the rapporteur on the opinion of the envi committee on this matter and, in these circumstances, i support the adoption of a resolution expressing parliament's position on measures to combat neurodegenerative diseases, in particular alzheimer's disease, by jointly planning research. neurodegenerative diseases are a major health problem in europe. advances in medical science and living standards in developed lands have led to an increase in life expectancy and the number of people afflicted with neurodegenerative diseases. it's a multi-faceted issue. there are aspects of the quality of life of those affected by these diseases, the impact that the disease has on those close to them or on the people who care for them. it is also a question of the sustainability of health systems, which will have to cope with an increasing number of patients as the ageing population increases the proportion of people who are no longer active in the labour market. the commission proposal focuses on research-related issues. the resolution we are proposing emphasizes both the results of coordinated research and the extent to which it will improve the present situation. i therefore call for a two-pronged approach, both in terms of scientific research and in terms of the quality of care that patients can receive. given the interest that parliament has shown over time in this area and the importance of this dossier, which is a pilot project for joint research programming, it is essential that parliament's position is taken into account in the drafting of the council conclusions. parliament must be involved in all future joint programming initiatives in the field of research and article 182 of the lisbon treaty provides an appropriate legal basis for future developments in this area.

the financial crisis led some member states to call on the eu for assistance (council regulation (ec) no 332/2002 of 18 february 2002) and on the international community for assistance (international monetary fund). this support should be directed both towards ensuring adequate conditions for protection and social inclusion and towards putting in place an enabling framework for economic development and job creation. between march 2008 and may 2009, the unemployment rate in the eu27 reached 8.9%, with the number of unemployed rising from 5.4 million to 21.5 million. the main concern of european citizens is the loss of jobs. the european union and its member states must be able to preserve existing jobs and create new ones, and this can be done by investing effectively in agriculture, education, health, transport and energy infrastructure. every european citizen who loses his job means a european family with lower incomes and an implicit decline in the quality of life. every job created means a family with a decent living and quality education for the younger generation. the success of the european model is determined by the quality of life of 500 million european citizens.
in writing. – much of the debate about honduras is focussed, understandably, on the political crisis - but the effects go far beyond politics. honduras is the second poorest country in latin america, and the economic and social impacts of the political crisis are hitting the 70 percent of the population which already lives in poverty. tourism has almost stopped, the suspension of foreign aid is having a direct effect on public investment, and overstretched and underequipped hospitals are struggling to cope - not just with the usual problems caused by poor sanitation, malnutrition and disease - but now also with the victims of increased street violence, including beatings and even killings by government forces. human rights and development organisations cannot do their valuable work because their staff are not protected by normal constitutional rights; instead, they face a curfew, detention without charge, and other violations of individual freedoms. this crisis extends far beyond the political deadlock and the battles between key political figures - it is about ordinary people whose day-to-day struggle has been made even harder during the last four months. every effort must be made to ensure free and fair elections and the immediate resumption of constitutional rights and foreign aid to alleviate the suffering of ordinary people.
european ombudsman. − mr president, thank you for this opportunity to address parliament on my annual report for 2008. i wish to thank the committee on petitions, and especially the chair, mrs mazzoni and the rapporteur, mrs paliadeli, for their helpful and constructive report. i enjoy an excellent working relationship with the committee. it offers me valuable support and advice whilst fully respecting my duty, as ombudsman, of impartiality and independence. parliament and the ombudsman both work to ensure that citizens and residents of the eu can enjoy their rights to the full. we do so in different ways. the ombudsman’s mandate is more limited; i can only deal with complaints against eu institutions and bodies, whilst the petitions committee can also examine what member states are doing. furthermore, parliament is a sovereign political body and can deal with petitions that request changes in the law, or even new laws. in contrast, my role is in dealing with complaints, helping complainants uncover maladministration and attempting to put it right. unlawful behaviour, when it falls within my mandate, is always a form of maladministration. however, it is not enough for eu institutions and bodies merely to follow the law. they must also act consistently and in good faith. they must act in accordance with the rules and principles which they have adopted, and they must demonstrate that they are service-minded, for example, by acting fairly, reasonably and courteously. indeed the generation and maintenance of a culture of service to citizens lies at the very heart of the principle of good administration. the ombudsman’s privileged relationship with parliament is key to ensuring results for citizens. unlike court rulings, an ombudsman’s decisions are not legally binding. i can only use the power of persuasion to convince eu institutions and bodies to follow my recommendations. where they refuse to do so, it is of fundamental importance that the ombudsman can turn to parliament to seek its support. for instance, when an institution does not comply with a recommendation in a case which raises fundamental questions of principle, i can issue a special report to parliament. one example from 2008 was the refusal of the commission to change its stance in an age discrimination case. i was gratified that parliament dealt with this report expeditiously and that mr martínez martínez’s report, adopted by plenary in may 2009 without a single vote against, reflected entirely the concerns i had raised. my annual report records the progress made in handling complaints, promoting good administration and providing information about the ombudsman’s role. as explained in its opening pages, strenuous efforts have been made to improve its user-friendliness so that readers can easily obtain a clear and comprehensive account of the ombudsman’s work. it has also now proven possible to publish the report much earlier in the year than before. in addition, a new six-page overview has been produced. this new publication records the most important results obtained for complainants, and highlights the main policy issues dealt with over the past year. the ombudsman closed a record number of enquiries in 2008 – 355 to be exact – with most taking less than a year. i am happy to say that the eu institutions and bodies have shown that in general they are keen to resolve issues that i bring to their attention. the increased number of friendly solutions and settlement of cases is both positive and praiseworthy. eight cases closed in 2008 exemplify best practice among the institutions and bodies in responding to issues i raised. the institutions and bodies concerned are the commission, the council, the court of justice, epso, olaf and the european aviation safety agency. the eight star cases are included in the report as models of good administrative behaviour for all institutions and bodies. let me briefly mention just two of these cases. the commission was constructive throughout the procedure concerning a payment dispute. as a result, the company concerned received more than eur 100 000 in outstanding payments. epso agreed to disclose to candidates, at their request, the evaluation criteria used in selection procedures, as well as a breakdown of individual marks. in 2008 the ombudsman registered a total of 3 406 complaints. this represents a 6% increase compared to 2007. in almost 80% of all cases registered, help was provided to the complainant by opening an inquiry, transferring the complaint to a competent body or giving advice. often such advice is to contact a member of the european network of ombudsmen. this network now consists of roughly 95 offices in 32 countries and includes the committee on petitions. one of its purposes is to facilitate the rapid transfer of complaints to the competent body. in 2008 for example, 191 complainants were either advised to petition parliament or their complaints were directly transferred to the committee on petitions. of course it is much better if complainants can identify the most appropriate avenue of redress the first time around. this helps avoid the frustration involved for citizens who are told that the body that they have turned to is not able to help them. it also means that complaints are resolved more promptly and effectively, thus ensuring that citizens can fully enjoy their rights under eu law. a very important initiative in this area came to fruition earlier this year. my office launched an entirely new website, including an interactive guide in all 23 languages, to help citizens address directly the body best equipped to deal with their complaint. this body may be my own department, the committee on petitions, the national ombudsman’s department in the complainant’s member state of origin, or the cross-border online network, solvit. so far this year over 23 000 people have used the guide to obtain advice. in 2008 by far the most common allegation i examined was lack of transparency in the eu administration. this allegation arose in 36% of all inquiries and included refusal of information or documents. it is with a certain degree of concern that i have noted this high percentage. an accountable and transparent eu administration is, and must remain, key to building citizens’ trust in the eu. of particular importance regarding transparency in 2008 was the commission’s proposal to reform regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 on public access to documents. the commission has proposed changes to this regulation, some of which would be very beneficial. however, in my estimation, some other proposed changes would result in citizens having access to fewer, not more, documents. the lisbon treaty changes the legal and political context of the regulation by giving citizens more opportunities to participate in the activities of the union. its entry into force will provide a good opportunity for the commission to submit a new proposal that would reflect this new reality and would strengthen the fundamental right of access to documents of the eu’s institutions and bodies. the support of parliament was crucial in securing the revision of the ombudsman’s statute in 2008. the changes effected strengthen the ombudsman’s powers of investigation, thereby ensuring that citizens can have full confidence in the ombudsman’s ability to conduct a thorough investigation of their complaints without restrictions. allow me to conclude by recalling that my task is to promote good administration in eu institutions and bodies. maximising transparency and accountability, and promoting and helping entrench a culture of service to citizens, are key factors in the fulfilment of this task. i am confident that our two institutions will continue to work closely in pursuit of the shared goal of helping citizens and residents to enjoy their rights fully in a transparent and accountable european union.

commission’s side, we have tried to contribute to this, and the new europa website does exactly that. it enhances visibility and citizens can easily find the ombudsman’s guide in a couple of clicks. so, all in all, in 2008 we saw both progress and possibilities for further improvements by our institutions. i would again like to thank mr diamandouros for his achievements and important work and mrs paliadeli for her excellent report.

vice-president of the commission. − madam president, first and foremost, i would like to note that the commission greatly welcomes the positive and constructive attitude of parliament on the process of adoption of the commission proposals for macro-financial assistance for four partner countries: armenia, georgia, serbia, and bosnia and herzegovina. the commission appreciates that the european parliament has opted for a procedure which allows for a vote – to take place tomorrow, already – on the reports for these four countries, without amendments to the commission’s proposals. parliament’s swift and decisive action will allow the council to adopt decisions on the four operations in the next few days, and the commission will then be in a position to start implementing the programmes. macro-financial assistance is by its very nature a short-term, crisis-response instrument and proposals for macro-financial assistance normally require rapid action. this is clearly the case for the countries we are examining today. armenia, georgia, serbia and bosnia are among those having suffered the most from the effects of the crisis, irrespective of the difference in their economic structures and level of development. they are also among those that have been implementing strong adjustment programmes with the support of the international monetary fund and those that have requested financial support from the eu. and the commission is indeed of the opinion that the conditions for extending macro-financial assistance to these countries are fully met. let me now turn to the instrument of macro-financial assistance and to its future under the lisbon treaty. the change brought by the lisbon treaty provides the ordinary legislative procedure for macro-financial assistance, with equal involvement of the european parliament and the council. at the same time, i think we all accept that a lengthy legislative procedure involving a long iterative process between the various institutions is not adapted to the macro-financial assistance instrument, or indeed to situations of crisis. therefore, the commission considers it crucial to examine how to deal with macro-financial assistance in the future, notably within the framework of the lisbon treaty. we would like to do this in close cooperation with the european parliament in order to ensure that in the future macro-financial assistance proposals are dealt with in a manner which on the one hand is rapid and allows for an effective crisis response, but on the other meets the requirements of the lisbon treaty for detailed scrutiny by legislators within the joint decision-making process. the commission has historically been in favour of a framework regulation governing the macro-financial assistance instrument. the commission services have started reflections at a technical level on the shape of such a framework regulation under the lisbon treaty. such a framework regulation could potentially have significant advantages. until such a framework regulation is adopted, individual commission proposals for macro-financial assistance programmes will be codecided on a case-by-case basis by the vice-president of the commission. − european research and innovation policy is mainly framed by the seventh research framework programme, covering the period 2007 to 2013, the competitiveness and innovation programme, covering the same period, and the cohesion funds, also covering the same period. in preparation for these three major programmes, the commission presented a long-term strategy and an action plan in 2005 and 2006. the action plan dates from 2005 and the broad innovation strategy from 2006. the results of these various programmes have been presented in extensive commission documents and have also been the subject of frequent debate in parliament. i am happy to make all these documents available to you again, madam president. it is not possible to present the content of the debate in a question and answer session, but i shall try to work out the main points. in the seventh framework programme for research we have seen a really remarkable increase in european r & d expenditure and a number of new instruments have been created, in particular the joint technology initiatives, which have proved to be extremely successful. the cohesion funds have been refocused and better targeted on the objective of promoting research and innovation, and it is really remarkable when you look at the numbers: the cohesion and structural funds have allocated eur 86 billion over the period in question to these tasks, which is at least 25% of the total structural and cohesion funds. a new instrument has been created within the framework of european structural policy, the jeremie initiative, which is primarily aimed at facilitating access to capital for small and medium-sized enterprises. this is being done in cooperation with the european investment fund. the programme for the promotion of innovation and competitiveness, for which i am responsible, is also essentially a programme for the creation of financial instruments. the majority of the funds are in fact used to facilitate access by smes to financial instruments designed to improve their capacity to innovate. as you know, our european policy for growth and employment does not have many quantitative objectives. but we have a quantitative target which has remained unchanged since 2000. that is the objective of spending 3% of gdp on research and development. we can already say today that this objective will not be achieved. however, looking at the percentages alone is a bit misleading, because in the european union, research and development expenditure increased by 14.8% in absolute terms between 2000 and 2006. this is a higher rate of increase than, for example, in the united states. however, we must say that the results are not satisfactory, which is why the council adopted a document entitled 'vision 2020' for the european research area in december last year, which deals with the question of how we can mobilise more funds for european research and development policy. i do not want to hide my concern that the current economic recession is putting the long-term strategy of promoting research and innovation at risk. the commission reacted very quickly to this threat in november 2008. the european economic recovery programme, which complements the member states' crisis-management measures and aims to provide impetus and to combat financial sector failures, focuses heavily on investment in research and development and investment promotion. i will give you three examples: the 'factory of the future' initiative, which is about modernising europe's industrial base with a budget of eur 1.2 billion, the 'energy efficient buildings' initiative, which has eur 1 billion, and the 'partnership for the development of green vehicles', which also has eur 1 billion for research and is supplemented by additional economic measures with expenditure of eur 4 billion. the commission has already started preparations for the next strategy for growth and employment. without giving away any secrets - because president barroso has already spoken about this in his guidelines - i can also say that research, development and innovation will play a very central role in this next strategy for growth and jobs. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we have very good, sometimes excellent research capacities. we also have very good results in technological development. but we could certainly be better when it comes to innovation. if we understand innovation as the practical application of research and development work to products, services, design, methods, in other words to anything where practical application is possible, then we see here a great potential to generate additional growth and additional employment in europe. the commission has therefore announced this year that it will present a so-called innovation act. an act is a new policy instrument that we have developed for the first time in relation to small and medium-sized enterprises - you remember the small business act - and we will be introducing an innovation act which brings together legislative measures, policy initiatives and politically binding guidelines in one big package. i have tried to steer the work in such a way that the next commission is free to decide when to present this innovation act. you'll understand that i can't anticipate this. that is a matter for the next commission to decide. but the preparatory work is already well advanced and i think it is safe to say that parliament will be able to deal with this innovation act next year. let me conclude by saying that in the last few years, we have seen progress on a broad front, everywhere, but it is very uneven. but here it is necessary to apply a fair approach. we cannot, for example, expect our new member states to spend the same amount of their gross national product on research, development and innovation. but i am very pleased to see that the new member states - especially those with the greatest economic need to catch up - are also catching up the fastest in this area, so i am looking at the overall trend in a positive way.

mr president, perhaps the most important lesson of the past enlargement is that we have brought into the union countries, markets, institutions and industrial assets, but we have left behind the hearts and minds of the people. i think that we have to avoid repeating this same experience in the future. we have also to prepare not only the acceding countries but also the existing member states. the famous enlargement fatigue says more about the lack of preparation of the present states – of the old member states, unprepared to live together with the new member states – rather than the indigestible character of the new member states. next, i think that we should, when speaking about the candidate countries, avoid any conditionality which is not linked directly to their capacity to be interoperable with us from the legal, institutional, political and cultural point of view and to compete with us within the internal market in the broader sense of this concept. we should not impose conditionalities which are not linked with these criteria. we should remember that enlargement is about a better future, not about a better past. we think too much about this past. thirdly, each country should indeed come in based on its merits. but we should also assess their capacity with their accession to contribute to a better situation in the region, more stability and more integration on a regional basis. management of expectations is also extremely important and i believe that perhaps in the future we should be a little bit more imaginative in trying to allow for some kind of gradual integration of a country for which full integration is not to be envisaged in the short term. my last point is that i believe we have to revisit the problem issue of our identity, our cultural and geopolitical identity, in order to know exactly what the limits of our enlargement are.
we are talking about enlargement with regard to the western balkans, turkey and iceland, there are three different cases: on the one hand we have the countries of the western balkans, which are far from meeting the economic and political criteria that the union expects. in these countries, however, public opinion and political elites are supportive of the integration objective and are very optimistic about accession. on the other hand, we have the case of iceland, a country that meets many of the economic and political criteria, but where public opinion and elites are deeply divided over this goal of membership. what seems to be binding only at this moment for the countries of the western balkans and iceland is that a deep economic crisis is giving them the courage to join. on the other hand, however, we have the case of turkey, whose european aspiration is not linked in any way to the economic cycle and is one of the most dynamic countries in the world, where there is a great debate, last time 45% of turks supported this objective. i want to distinguish these three situations because the western balkans, iceland and turkey, respectively, are from the perspective of integration, three different situations. on the other hand, it is good to treat these cases beyond a bilateral political logic. in my view, differences between the member states and the countries that could become candidates cannot be used by either the member states or third countries to block a european path. i believe that the merits of each country and the public consensus are the only benchmarks of a european path.

citizens and the environment in the european union must benefit from the protection afforded by the ban on smoking in public places. we cannot ignore the fact that, at this moment, smoking remains one of the most important causes of illness and death. we fight dangerous epidemics with all our might and invent complicated and expensive vaccines to protect us from new viruses, but the effort to protect our children, families, and the environment from the harm of smoking is much more within our reach. simple logic, if not the use of concepts such as the right of the non-smoking majority, should convince us to treat this effort as a priority. recent studies show that smoking bans in north america and europe have led to rapid reductions in serious health problems, and this effect was seen almost immediately after the introduction of the smoking ban. in countries that have completely banned smoking in public places, the positive impact on health has been due to a combination of factors. these include eliminating secondhand smoke for smokers and reducing secondhand smoke for non-smokers. i would like to make one crucial point: smokers are a minority in the european union. of course, no one can suggest that individuals be given a ban on smoking, even in the name of principles that we all support, such as a well-protected public health or an environment free of sources of pollution. at the same time, however, the majority of non-smokers want an environment free of cigarette smoke. this truth should guide us in developing and supporting anti-smoking legislation. since the evidence suggests that smokers tend to quit smoking with the support of these supporting measures, i believe that we need to strengthen anti-smoking legislation as part of the community tobacco control policy in order to make a concrete contribution to improving public health in the european union.

in writing. the eu budget for 2010 is the last budget approved under the treaty of nice. the new treaty gives the european parliament greater power and the final say in adopting the budget. parliament and the council will have equal powers as legislators in areas such as agriculture, energy, immigration, justice and home affairs, health and the structural funds, including, of course, their budgets. the 2010 budget allocates significant percentages to conservation and management of natural resources, social and economic cohesion, growth and employment, competitiveness and innovation, regional development, agriculture and rural development. the european economic recovery plan is reflected in the eu budget for 2010 with €2.4 billion to finance strategic projects in energy, transport, the development of broadband networks in rural areas and support for rural communities. i welcome the fact that the european parliament has managed to allocate eur 300 million to support milk producers. the economic crisis has affected member states' gdp and will affect member states' contributions to the eu budget. i hope that the mid-term review of the 2007-2013 financial framework in 2010 will allow member states to better absorb structural funds, especially in the area of transport and energy efficiency of housing.
